Part I · Welcome to Ricing

What Ricing Is (and How a Linux Desktop Works)

Welcome. This book assumes you know nothing: not Linux internals, not Qt, not programming. By the last page you'll be able to design a desktop in your head (or on paper, or from a screenshot you love) and build it, piece by piece, with Quickshell.

This first chapter has no code. It gives you the mental map. Every later chapter hangs off it, so don't skip it.

What "ricing" means#

Ricing is customizing how your desktop looks and behaves: bars, colors, fonts, widgets, animations, wallpapers, lock screens. The word comes from car culture (making a car look fast with body kits). In the Linux world it simply means making your desktop yours. Communities like r/unixporn are full of "rices".

A rice usually has these parts:

Part What it is Examples of tools
Compositor / window manager Places windows on the screen, handles workspaces and keybinds Hyprland, Sway, niri, river, KDE's KWin
Bar / panel The strip with workspaces, clock, battery, tray Waybar, Polybar, Quickshell
Launcher Search box to open apps rofi, wofi, fuzzel, Quickshell
Notification daemon Shows popups when apps send notifications dunst, mako, swaync, Quickshell
Lock screen Asks for your password swaylock, hyprlock, Quickshell
Widgets Clocks, music players, system monitors on the desktop eww, conky, Quickshell
Theme Colors, fonts, icons, cursor matugen, pywal, GTK/Qt themes

Notice how often Quickshell appears. That's the point: Quickshell isn't "a bar". It's a toolkit for building every one of those shell components, all in one language, sharing one set of colors and one state. A single Quickshell config can replace Waybar + rofi + dunst + swaylock + eww.

How a Linux desktop is put together#

When you look at your screen, several programs are cooperating. Here is the stack from the hardware up:

The kernel and drivers#

The very bottom. It talks to the hardware: your GPU, keyboard, battery, speakers. You rarely touch it while ricing, but files like /sys/class/backlight/ (screen brightness) and /sys/class/power_supply/ (battery) come from here.

System services and D-Bus#

Background programs (daemons) that manage things:

  • PipeWire (with WirePlumber) handles all audio: volume, which speaker, per-app streams.
  • UPower watches batteries and power.
  • NetworkManager handles Wi-Fi and Ethernet.
  • BlueZ handles Bluetooth.
  • MPRIS isn't a daemon but a standard: every media player (Spotify, Firefox, mpv) announces itself on D-Bus so others can control it.

D-Bus is the "telephone network" these programs use to talk. When your bar shows the volume, it's really asking PipeWire over its own protocol, or asking UPower over D-Bus. Quickshell has these connections built in, which is why it can show live battery and volume without running scripts.

The compositor#

On modern Linux (Wayland), the compositor is the most important program. It:

  • receives every frame from every app and composes them into the final image,
  • decides where windows go (tiling, floating, workspaces),
  • owns the keyboard and mouse and sends input to the right window,
  • runs your keybinds.

Hyprland, Sway, niri and river are compositors. If you used Linux years ago you might know X11, the older system, where the "X server" did this job and a separate "window manager" placed windows. On Wayland, compositor and window manager are one program.

Wayland vs X11

Quickshell is built for Wayland. Most of its special features (bars that reserve space, lock screens, overlays) use Wayland protocols. It can show plain windows on X11, but this book assumes Wayland, and every modern ricing compositor is Wayland.

Apps and the shell layer#

Normal apps make normal windows. A shell (in the desktop sense, not the terminal sense) is the set of programs that make up the desktop itself: the bar, the dock, the launcher, notifications. On GNOME this is gnome-shell; on KDE it's Plasma. When you rice a compositor like Hyprland, you build your own shell, and Quickshell is the tool for that.

Two meanings of "shell"

In this book, shell almost always means desktop shell (bars, panels, widgets). The terminal shell (bash, zsh, fish) is the program in your terminal that runs commands. When we mean that one, we'll say "terminal" or "bash".

Layer shell: how a bar becomes a bar#

A normal app window can be moved and tiled by the compositor. A bar mustn't be: it has to stick to the top edge, stay above windows, and push tiled windows down so they don't cover it. Wayland solves this with the layer shell protocol (wlr-layer-shell). A program asks the compositor for a layer surface and says:

  • anchor me to the top/bottom/left/right edges,
  • put me on layer Background, Bottom, Top or Overlay,
  • reserve N pixels (the exclusive zone) so windows avoid me,
  • give me (or don't give me) keyboard focus.

In Quickshell this is the PanelWindow type plus the WlrLayershell settings. You'll use it constantly from Your First Shell and the Dev Loop onward.

What Quickshell actually is#

Quickshell is a program (quickshell, also installed as qs) that:

  1. Reads a folder of QML files you write (your "config").
  2. Creates the windows, widgets and connections those files describe.
  3. Watches the files: when you save, it reloads instantly (hot reload).
  4. Gives your QML extra building blocks that plain Qt doesn't have: - Windows: PanelWindow, FloatingWindow, PopupWindow, and per-monitor copies with Variants. - System services: Pipewire audio, Mpris media, UPower battery, SystemTray, NotificationServer, Bluetooth, Networking, PamContext passwords, PolkitAgent, Greetd. - Compositor integration: Hyprland, I3 (Sway), Niri, plus generic ToplevelManager. - I/O: run commands with Process, read and write files with FileView, expose commands with IpcHandler.

What QML is#

QML (Qt Modeling Language) is a declarative language for user interfaces. Instead of writing steps ("create a box, then set its color, then when the volume changes update the box…"), you describe what things are:

Rectangle {
    width: 200
    height: 20
    color: Audio.muted ? "red" : "green"
}

That rectangle is always red when muted and green otherwise. You never write "update the color": QML tracks it for you. This idea, the binding, is why QML is so good for live desktop widgets. Bindings: The Heart of QML is devoted to it.

QML comes from Qt (pronounced "cute"), a huge, mature toolkit used by KDE Plasma, many embedded screens and car dashboards. Quickshell runs on Qt 6, so everything in Qt Quick (animations, effects, layouts, text rendering) is available to you.

Quickshell vs the alternatives#

Tool Language What it can build Live data Notes
Waybar JSON + CSS Bars only Built-in modules + scripts Easy, but limited to what modules exist
eww Yuck + GTK CSS Widgets, bars Mostly polling scripts Flexible but scripts everywhere
AGS / Astal JS/TS + GTK Everything Native libraries Powerful, heavier toolchain
Quickshell QML + JS Everything Native services, no polling Hot reload, GPU animations, compositor integrations

The rices you'll learn from#

These popular configs are built with Quickshell. You'll recognize their techniques as the book goes on, and Reading Other People's Rices shows you how to read their source.

  • end-4 / dots-hyprland ("illogical-impulse") — a Material You desktop with a bar, left and right sidebars (AI chat, quick settings, notifications), an overview with live window previews, a dock, OSDs, a cheatsheet and a lock screen.
  • Caelestia — a shell built from "drawers" that slide out of the screen edges, with smooth shape morphing, a media dashboard and an audio visualizer.
  • Noctalia and DankMaterialShell — complete, distributable shells with settings apps, aimed at being installed by others.
  • JaKooLit's Hyprland-Dots — a popular all-in-one Hyprland setup that mixes classic tools (Waybar, rofi) with Quickshell components, a good model for adopting Quickshell gradually.

How this book is organized#

  • Part I (you are here): Linux basics, installing, your first shell, editor setup.
  • Part II: the QML language. Every concept, from one property to components and imports.
  • Part III: Qt Quick. Drawing, layout, input, animation, effects.
  • Part IV: Quickshell concepts. Windows, monitors, popups, singletons, processes, files, IPC, compositors, services.
  • Part V: design and architecture. How big rices are organized, theming from wallpapers, motion design.
  • Part VI: build-along projects. Nineteen real components, start to finish.
  • Part VII: mastery. Debugging, performance, a recipe cookbook.
  • Qt reference: the Qt types you'll use, with their important properties.
  • API reference: every Quickshell type, with every property, function, signal and enum, plus complete examples.
  • Glossary and A–Z index: look up any word.
How to read

Read Parts I–III in order and type every example yourself; copying and pasting teaches far less. From Part IV on, read in order or jump to what you need, using the API reference as your dictionary. Press / anywhere to search.

Before the next chapter

Open a terminal and run echo $XDG_SESSION_TYPE. If it prints wayland, you're ready. If it prints x11, log out and choose a Wayland session (Hyprland, Sway, niri…) on your login screen.

Part I · Welcome to Ricing

Linux Survival Kit for Ricers

Ricing means living in config files and the terminal. This chapter teaches exactly the Linux you need, nothing more. If you already know cd, ~/.config, chmod +x and environment variables, skim the headings and move on.

The terminal in five minutes#

The terminal runs a terminal shell (bash, zsh or fish), a program that reads commands you type. A command is a program name followed by arguments:

ls -la ~/.config
# ^   ^    ^
# |   |    └── argument: which folder
# |   └─────── option (flag): -l long format, -a show hidden files
# └─────────── program: list files

Commands you'll use constantly:

Command Does Example
pwd Print the folder you're in pwd
cd DIR Change folder (cd alone = home, cd - = back) cd ~/.config/quickshell
ls List files (-a hidden, -l details) ls -la
mkdir -p DIR Make a folder (and its parents) mkdir -p ~/.config/quickshell/bar
cp SRC DST Copy (-r for folders) cp -r myshell myshell.bak
mv SRC DST Move or rename mv old.qml New.qml
rm FILE Delete (-r folders). There's no trash! rm test.qml
cat FILE Print a file cat /sys/class/power_supply/BAT0/capacity
less FILE Scroll through a file (q quits) less ~/.config/hypr/hyprland.conf
nano FILE Simple terminal editor (Ctrl+O save, Ctrl+X exit) nano shell.qml
grep TEXT FILE Find lines containing text (-r recursive) grep -r "PanelWindow" ~/.config/quickshell
which CMD Where is a program? Is it installed? which matugen
man CMD Manual page man brightnessctl
CMD --help Short help qs --help

Handy keys: Tab autocompletes names, ↑ recalls previous commands, Ctrl+C stops the running command, Ctrl+R searches history.

Paths: where things live#

A path is an address of a file. / is the root of everything. ~ is shorthand for your home folder (/home/yourname).

  • Absolute path starts with /: /usr/share/icons
  • Relative path starts from where you are: modules/bar/Bar.qml
  • . means "this folder", .. means "parent folder"
  • Files starting with . are hidden (~/.config is hidden; use ls -a)

The folders that matter for ricing:

Path What's there
~/.config/ Per-user configuration. Your rice lives here.
~/.config/quickshell/ Quickshell configs
~/.config/hypr/ Hyprland config (hyprland.conf or Lua config)
~/.local/share/ Per-user data (fonts in fonts/, icons in icons/, app files)
~/.local/state/ Per-user state (history, last-used things)
~/.cache/ Throwaway cache (generated colors, thumbnails)
/usr/share/applications/ .desktop files: the list of installed apps
/usr/share/icons/ Icon themes
/usr/share/fonts/ System fonts
/sys/class/backlight/ Screen brightness (read/write numbers)
/sys/class/power_supply/ Battery and charger info
/proc/ Live kernel info: /proc/meminfo (RAM), /proc/stat (CPU)
/etc/ System-wide config (needs root to edit)
/run/user/1000/ ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR) Sockets for your session (Hyprland's IPC lives here)
The XDG folders

~/.config, ~/.local/share, ~/.local/state and ~/.cache are the XDG base directories. Quickshell gives you helpers to build paths inside them for your shell: Quickshell.dataPath(), Quickshell.statePath(), Quickshell.cachePath().

Files, permissions and scripts#

Every file has an owner and permissions: read, write, execute. To run a script you wrote, it must be executable:

nano ~/.config/quickshell/myshell/scripts/hello.sh   # write the script
chmod +x ~/.config/quickshell/myshell/scripts/hello.sh  # make it executable
~/.config/quickshell/myshell/scripts/hello.sh           # run it

A shell script starts with a shebang line that says which interpreter runs it:

scripts/hello.sh#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "Hello from a script. You passed: $1"

sudo runs a command as root (administrator). You need it to install packages or edit files in /etc, and almost never for ricing your own config. If you find yourself writing sudo inside your Quickshell config, stop and rethink.

Packages#

On Arch-based systems (Arch, CachyOS, EndeavourOS, Garuda):

sudo pacman -Syu                 # update everything
sudo pacman -S brightnessctl     # install a package from the official repos
pacman -Ss matugen               # search
pacman -Qi quickshell            # info about an installed package
paru -S quickshell-git           # install from the AUR (needs an AUR helper: paru or yay)

Other distros: apt (Debian/Ubuntu), dnf (Fedora), zypper (openSUSE), nix (NixOS). The package names in this book are Arch names; search your distro if one differs.

Processes#

A process is a running program. Your Quickshell config runs as a process, and it can start other processes (that's what Process does).

pgrep -a qs              # is Quickshell running? shows PID + command
pkill qs                 # stop it (sends SIGTERM)
kill -9 12345            # force-kill PID 12345 (last resort)
top                      # live CPU/RAM per process (q to quit); htop/btop are nicer

Every process has:

  • arguments (the command line),
  • standard output (stdout), where it prints normal text,
  • standard error (stderr), where it prints errors,
  • standard input (stdin), where it can read text,
  • an exit code: 0 means success, anything else means failure.

When Quickshell runs a command for your bar, it reads its stdout. That's how you'll get CPU usage, Wi-Fi names and more.

Pipes#

The | symbol sends one command's output into another's input:

cat /proc/meminfo | grep MemAvailable      # just the line we want
nmcli -t -f ACTIVE,SSID dev wifi | grep '^yes'   # the connected Wi-Fi network

Pipes are a feature of the terminal shell, not of programs. To use them from Quickshell you must run them through sh -c "…" (covered in Running Commands with Process).

Environment variables#

Variables that every process inherits, used for settings:

echo $HOME                       # /home/you
echo $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR            # /run/user/1000
echo $HYPRLAND_INSTANCE_SIGNATURE   # set when running under Hyprland
echo $WAYLAND_DISPLAY            # wayland-1
env | less                       # all of them
MYVAR=hello qs                   # run qs with an extra variable

In QML you read them with Quickshell.env(): Quickshell.env("HOME").

D-Bus, briefly#

You'll rarely use D-Bus directly (Quickshell's services hide it), but knowing it exists helps with debugging:

busctl --user list | grep -i mpris        # which media players are running?
playerctl -l                              # same, friendlier (MPRIS)
busctl --user tree org.freedesktop.Notifications   # who owns the notification name?

There are two buses: the session bus (your user's programs: media players, notifications, tray) and the system bus (system services: UPower, NetworkManager, BlueZ).

systemd user services#

Many desktop pieces run as systemd user services. Useful commands:

systemctl --user status pipewire wireplumber    # audio stack OK?
systemctl status upower NetworkManager bluetooth # system services OK?
systemctl --user restart wireplumber            # fix weird audio states
journalctl --user -b -u pipewire                # logs of a user service this boot

You can even run Quickshell itself as a user service, covered in Sharing and Maintaining Your Rice.

Your compositor's config#

You'll edit your compositor's config to start Quickshell and add keybinds. Locations:

Compositor Config file Reload
Hyprland ~/.config/hypr/hyprland.conf (newer versions also accept a Lua config) auto on save, or hyprctl reload
Sway ~/.config/sway/config swaymsg reload
niri ~/.config/niri/config.kdl auto on save
river ~/.config/river/init restart

Each has a command-line tool for querying and controlling it: hyprctl, swaymsg, niri msg, riverctl. Try hyprctl monitors or niri msg outputs to see your screens.

Fonts and icons#

Text and icons are a huge part of a rice.

fc-list | grep -i "jetbrains"        # is a font installed? what is its exact family name?
fc-list : family | sort -u | less    # all font family names
fc-cache -fv                         # refresh after copying fonts into ~/.local/share/fonts

The family name printed by fc-list is exactly what you write in QML's font.family. Icons come from icon themes (Papirus, Adwaita, Tela…) in /usr/share/icons or ~/.local/share/icons, and from icon fonts like Material Symbols or Nerd Fonts. Fonts and Icons covers both.

Backups and git#

Before big changes, copy your config:

cp -r ~/.config/quickshell/myshell ~/.config/quickshell/myshell.bak-$(date +%F)

Better: put it under git, so every working state is saved and you can always go back:

cd ~/.config/quickshell/myshell
git init
git add -A && git commit -m "bar works"
# … later, after breaking something:
git diff            # what changed?
git checkout -- .   # throw away uncommitted changes
Practice
  1. Make the folder ~/.config/quickshell/playground.
  2. Print your battery percentage with cat /sys/class/power_supply/BAT*/capacity (desktops have none, which is fine).
  3. Find the exact family name of one installed monospace font with fc-list.
  4. Run hyprctl monitors (or your compositor's equivalent) and note your monitor names, like eDP-1 or DP-2. You'll use them later.
Part I · Welcome to Ricing

Installing Quickshell and Your Toolbox

Installing Quickshell#

Distro Command
Arch, CachyOS, EndeavourOS sudo pacman -S quickshell (stable) or paru -S quickshell-git (newest)
Fedora sudo dnf copr enable errornointernet/quickshell then sudo dnf install quickshell
NixOS add pkgs.quickshell to environment.systemPackages, or use the upstream flake
Gentoo GURU overlay, gui-apps/quickshell
Anything else build from source with CMake and Qt ≥ 6.6 (see the repo's BUILD.md)

Check it works:

qs --version
# quickshell 0.3.x …

quickshell and qs are the same program; this book writes qs.

Forks: noctalia-qs and others

Some shells ship their own build of Quickshell. For example, noctalia-qs (used by the Noctalia shell) is a fork that adds extra modules such as Quickshell.Niri and Quickshell.DWL. A fork replaces the qs binary, so you can only have one installed at a time. Everything in this book works on upstream Quickshell. Types marked "noctalia-qs fork only" in the API reference need that fork. Check what you have with pacman -Qo $(which qs).

Fonts#

Install at least one good UI font, one monospace font and one icon font:

# UI + mono fonts
sudo pacman -S inter-font ttf-jetbrains-mono-nerd ttf-roboto noto-fonts noto-fonts-emoji

# Material Symbols (the icon font end-4, Caelestia and most M3 rices use)
paru -S ttf-material-symbols-variable-git
fc-list | grep -i "material symbols"     # should list Rounded / Outlined / Sharp

Icon theme#

App icons in launchers, docks and trays come from an icon theme:

sudo pacman -S papirus-icon-theme

You'll tell Quickshell which theme to use with a pragma in Shell Structure, Pragmas and Reloading.

Qt modules#

Your distro's quickshell package pulls in what it needs, but rices commonly use a few extra Qt modules:

sudo pacman -S qt6-declarative qt6-svg qt6-imageformats qt6-multimedia qt6-5compat qt6-wayland
Module Why you might need it
qt6-svg SVG icons and images
qt6-imageformats WebP, TIFF and other wallpaper formats
qt6-multimedia Video wallpapers, playing sounds
qt6-5compat Qt5Compat.GraphicalEffects, used by older configs

Helper tools used in this book#

None of these are required to learn, but the projects use them:

Tool Package (Arch) Used for
brightnessctl brightnessctl Change screen brightness
wpctl wireplumber Change volume from keybinds
playerctl playerctl Media keys
nmcli networkmanager Wi-Fi (if you don't use the Networking module)
bluez bluez bluez-utils Bluetooth
upower upower Battery
powerprofilesctl power-profiles-daemon Power profiles
cliphist, wl-copy cliphist wl-clipboard Clipboard history
grim, slurp grim slurp Screenshots
matugen matugen (AUR or extra) Generate colors from your wallpaper
qalc libqalculate Calculator in the launcher
hyprsunset / wlsunset hyprsunset Night light 
sudo pacman -S brightnessctl wireplumber playerctl networkmanager bluez bluez-utils upower \
               power-profiles-daemon cliphist wl-clipboard grim slurp libqalculate
paru -S matugen-bin

Make sure services are running#

systemctl --user status pipewire wireplumber     # audio
systemctl status upower                          # battery
systemctl status NetworkManager                  # network
systemctl status bluetooth                       # bluetooth (enable: sudo systemctl enable --now bluetooth)

Stop the things Quickshell will replace#

Only one program can be the notification daemon, and two bars would overlap. While learning you can keep your old setup running and build in a separate config. When you switch over, remove these from your compositor's autostart:

pkill waybar; pkill dunst; pkill mako; pkill swaync
Learn safely

You can run Quickshell next to your existing bar. Your experiments live in ~/.config/quickshell/<name>/ and start with qs -c <name>. Nothing changes permanently until you edit your compositor's autostart.

Checklist
  • qs --version prints a version.
  • fc-list | grep -i "material symbols rounded" prints something.
  • wpctl status shows your speakers.
  • upower -e lists devices (on a laptop you should see a battery).
Part I · Welcome to Ricing

Your First Shell and the Dev Loop

Time to put something on the screen. By the end of this chapter you'll have a working bar and know the edit → save → see loop you'll use for the rest of the book.

Where configs live#

Quickshell looks for configs in ~/.config/quickshell/:

~/.config/quickshell/
├── playground/
│   └── shell.qml        ← a NAMED config: `qs -c playground`
└── myshell/
    ├── shell.qml        ← every config has a shell.qml entry point
    ├── Bar.qml
    └── ...

You can also put a single shell.qml directly in ~/.config/quickshell/, and plain qs runs it as the "default" config.

Default config hides named configs

If ~/.config/quickshell/shell.qml exists, Quickshell treats the whole folder as one config and ignores the subfolders, so qs -c playground will fail. Use either one default config or named subfolders, not both. This book uses named configs.

We'll use a named config called playground so your experiments never collide with anything else.

Step 1: the smallest possible shell#

mkdir -p ~/.config/quickshell/playground
nano ~/.config/quickshell/playground/shell.qml     # or your editor from the next chapter

Type this (don't paste; typing builds memory):

~/.config/quickshell/playground/shell.qmlimport Quickshell
import QtQuick

PanelWindow {
    anchors.top: true
    anchors.left: true
    anchors.right: true
    implicitHeight: 32

    Text {
        anchors.centerIn: parent
        text: "Hello, rice!"
    }
}

Run it:

qs -c playground

A white bar appears along the top of your screen with "Hello, rice!" in the middle, and your tiled windows move down to make room.

What each line means#

Line Meaning
import Quickshell Load Quickshell's types (PanelWindow comes from here).
import QtQuick Load Qt's basic visual types (Text, Rectangle, …).
PanelWindow { Create a PanelWindow: a window glued to screen edges (a layer-shell surface).
anchors.top: true … Glue it to the top, left and right edges, so it stretches across the screen.
implicitHeight: 32 It's 32 pixels tall.
Text { … } A child object: a piece of text drawn inside the window.
anchors.centerIn: parent Center the text inside its parent (the window).
text: "Hello, rice!" What the text says.

Step 2: hot reload#

Leave qs running. Change the text to "It reloads!" and save. The bar updates instantly, no restart. This is hot reload, and it's the most important productivity feature you have.

Now break something on purpose: delete the closing } at the end and save. Look at the terminal:

ERROR: Failed to load configuration
  file:///home/you/.config/quickshell/playground/shell.qml:14:1: Expected token `}'

The bar on screen keeps showing the last working version, and a small popup tells you the reload failed. Put the brace back and save again: everything recovers. You can't break your desktop by saving a bad file.

Read the error

Errors always give file:line:column. Line 14, column 1 means "look at the start of line 14". Most beginner errors are a missing }, a missing import, or a typo in a type name (Rectange).

Step 3: make it look like a rice#

~/.config/quickshell/playground/shell.qmlimport Quickshell
import QtQuick

PanelWindow {
    anchors { top: true; left: true; right: true }   // the same three lines, grouped
    margins { top: 6; left: 10; right: 10 }          // float it away from the edges
    implicitHeight: 36
    color: "transparent"                             // window itself is invisible…

    Rectangle {                                      // …we draw our own rounded background
        anchors.fill: parent
        radius: 12
        color: "#1e1e2e"
        border.color: "#313244"
        border.width: 1

        Text {
            anchors.left: parent.left
            anchors.leftMargin: 14
            anchors.verticalCenter: parent.verticalCenter
            text: "  my rice"
            color: "#cba6f7"
            font.pixelSize: 14
            font.bold: true
        }

        Text {
            id: clock
            anchors.centerIn: parent
            color: "#cdd6f4"
            font.pixelSize: 14
            text: Qt.formatDateTime(new Date(), "hh:mm:ss")

            Timer {                                   // re-run every second
                interval: 1000
                running: true
                repeat: true
                onTriggered: clock.text = Qt.formatDateTime(new Date(), "hh:mm:ss")
            }
        }
    }
}

Save. You now have a floating, rounded, dark bar with a ticking clock. In Timers, Dates and Time you'll replace the Timer with the better SystemClock.

The qs command line#

Command What it does
qs Run the default config ~/.config/quickshell/shell.qml
qs -c NAME Run ~/.config/quickshell/NAME/shell.qml
qs -p PATH Run a config from any path (a folder or a .qml file)
qs -d Daemonize: run in the background and free the terminal
qs --allow-duplicate Allow a second copy of the same config (by default qs refuses to start a config that's already running)
qs list List running instances
qs kill / qs kill -c NAME Stop an instance
qs log -c NAME / -f Show (or follow) the log of a background instance
qs ipc show List IPC commands your config exposes (IPC, Keybinds and Sockets)
qs ipc call TARGET FUNC ARGS… Call one
qs -v / -vv More verbose logging (INFO / DEBUG internal logs)
qs ipc listen TARGET SIGNAL Print every time an IPC signal fires
qs --help Everything else

Logging from QML#

Print anything to the terminal with console.log:

Text {
    text: "hi"
    Component.onCompleted: console.log("Text created, width is", width)
}

Output: INFO qml: Text created, width is 14. Use console.warn and console.error for louder messages. This is your main debugging tool; Debugging covers more.

Running it for real#

When your config is ready to be your daily shell, start it from your compositor:

~/.config/hypr/hyprland.confexec-once = qs -c myshell
~/.config/sway/configexec qs -c myshell
~/.config/niri/config.kdlspawn-at-startup "qs" "-c" "myshell"

To restart it while developing: qs kill -c myshell; qs -c myshell -d.

Common first-day problems#

Problem Fix
qs: command not found Quickshell isn't installed or not on PATH. Reinstall.
module "Quickshell" is not installed Broken install or Qt version mismatch: reinstall quickshell (and its -git deps).
Nothing appears, no error Did you set a size (implicitHeight)? A zero-size window isn't shown.
Bar appears on the wrong monitor Normal: you haven't chosen a screen yet. Multiple Monitors with Variants fixes it.
Windows don't move out of the way The compositor ignores the exclusive zone for floating windows; tiled ones move.
Text is invisible Default text color is black: on a black background set color.
Exercises
  1. Move the bar to the bottom of the screen.
  2. Make a vertical bar: anchor left, top and bottom, and use implicitWidth: 44 instead of implicitHeight.
  3. Add a third Text on the right side showing your username. Hint: anchors.right: parent.right and Quickshell.env("USER").
  4. Break the file in three different ways and read each error message.
Part I · Welcome to Ricing

Setting Up Your Editor

You can write QML in any text editor, but autocomplete and inline errors make learning much faster. QML has a language server, qmlls, and Quickshell can feed it everything it needs to know about Quickshell's types.

Step 1: tell Quickshell to help qmlls#

Create an empty file called .qmlls.ini next to your shell.qml:

touch ~/.config/quickshell/playground/.qmlls.ini

Now start (or restart) qs -c playground. Quickshell sees the file and writes the correct import paths into it. Leave it alone after that, and add it to .gitignore if you use git, because its contents are machine-specific.

Step 2: install qmlls#

It ships with Qt's declarative module:

sudo pacman -S qt6-declarative          # provides /usr/lib/qt6/bin/qmlls
ls /usr/lib/qt6/bin/qmlls               # some distros name it qmlls6

If your editor can't find it, add Qt's bin folder to your PATH or point the editor at the full path.

Step 3: configure your editor#

VS Code / VSCodium#

  1. Install the official Qt Qml extension (publisher: theqtcompany).
  2. In settings, enable its qmlls option and, if needed, set the qmlls path to /usr/lib/qt6/bin/qmlls.
  3. Open your config folder (not a single file).

Neovim#

~/.config/nvim/lua/lsp.lua-- with nvim-lspconfig
require("lspconfig").qmlls.setup({
  cmd = { "/usr/lib/qt6/bin/qmlls" },
})
-- Neovim 0.11+ built-in:
-- vim.lsp.config("qmlls", { cmd = { "/usr/lib/qt6/bin/qmlls" } }); vim.lsp.enable("qmlls")

Install the Treesitter parser qmljs for syntax highlighting.

Helix#

~/.config/helix/languages.toml[language-server.qmlls]
command = "/usr/lib/qt6/bin/qmlls"

[[language]]
name = "qml"
language-servers = ["qmlls"]

Zed, Kate, Emacs#

Each supports LSP. Register qmlls for *.qml files. Kate ships with QML support enabled.

What you get#

  • Autocomplete for properties: type Rect and get Rectangle; inside it, type col and get color.
  • Red squiggles for unknown types and typos.
  • "Go to definition" for your own components.
  • Hover documentation for many types.
qmlls is not the judge

qmlls sometimes marks valid Quickshell code as an error, especially singletons, import qs.… paths and attached properties. If qs runs your config without complaint, the code is fine. The qs terminal output is the source of truth.

Formatting#

Qt ships qmlformat to auto-format QML:

/usr/lib/qt6/bin/qmlformat -i shell.qml     # -i = edit in place

Most editor QML extensions can run it on save. Consistent formatting makes braces easy to match, which prevents the most common beginner error.

A comfortable layout#

Put your editor and a terminal running qs -c playground side by side, with the bar visible on screen. Edit, save, glance. That loop, measured in seconds, is how every rice in this book was built.

Check your setup

In shell.qml, type PanelW and confirm autocomplete offers PanelWindow. Then type a wrong property name like colr: "red" and confirm both your editor and qs complain.

Part II · The QML Language

Objects and Properties

Everything in QML is built from two ideas: objects and properties. Master these and the rest of the language is detail.

Objects#

An object is a thing: a rectangle, a piece of text, a window, a timer, a battery. You create one by writing its type name followed by curly braces:

Rectangle {
}

That's a complete, valid object: a Rectangle with all default settings (which happen to make it invisible: zero size, white).

Rules for type names:

  • They start with a capital letter: Rectangle, Text, PanelWindow.
  • They come from imports (import QtQuick gives you Rectangle) or from your own files (Pill.qml gives you Pill).

Properties#

A property is a named setting of an object. Inside the braces you write name: value:

Rectangle {
    width: 120
    height: 40
    color: "orange"
    radius: 8
}

Now the rectangle is 120×40 pixels, orange, with rounded corners. Each line is a property assignment: the property name, a colon, then a value.

  • Property names start with a lowercase letter: width, color, implicitHeight.
  • Order doesn't matter. QML isn't a list of steps.
  • One property per line. To put several on one line, separate them with ;:
Rectangle { width: 120; height: 40; color: "orange" }

Every object has a type, and every type has a fixed set of properties#

You can only set properties the type actually has. Rectangle has color, radius, border, plus everything from Item (width, height, x, y, opacity…). Text has text, font, color, wrapMode…

Rectangle {
    text: "hi"      // ERROR: Rectangle has no property "text"
}
Cannot assign to non-existent property "text"

How do you know which properties a type has? That's what the reference is for: the Qt reference chapters for Qt types, and the API reference for Quickshell types. Every property is listed there with its type and meaning.

Nesting: children#

Put an object inside another object's braces and it becomes a child:

Rectangle {                 // parent
    width: 200; height: 100
    color: "#1e1e2e"

    Text {                  // child of the Rectangle
        text: "inside"
        color: "white"
    }

    Rectangle {             // another child
        x: 150; y: 60
        width: 40; height: 30
        color: "tomato"
    }
}

Children are:

  • positioned relative to their parent. x: 150 means 150 px from the parent's left edge, not the screen's.
  • drawn on top of their parent, and later children on top of earlier ones.
  • moved, hidden and faded with their parent. Set the parent's opacity: 0.5 and the children fade too.

The whole file is a tree of objects. The top object is the root, and a file can have only one.

Declaring your own properties#

You can add new properties to any object with the property keyword:

Rectangle {
    property int volume: 40            // type, name, default value
    property string label: "Volume"
    property bool muted: false

    width: 200; height: 24
    color: muted ? "grey" : "steelblue"
}

Syntax: property <type> <name>: <initial value>. The initial value is optional (property int volume defaults to 0).

Why declare properties? To store state ("is the menu open?") and to create an API for your own components, which you'll do in Components, Files and Imports. A property you declare behaves exactly like built-in ones: you can bind to it, react when it changes, and set it from outside.

Property modifiers#

Modifier Meaning Example
readonly Can't be assigned after creation; usually a computed value readonly property bool loud: volume > 80
required Whoever creates this object must set it required property string title
default Children written inside this object go into this property default property alias content: box.data
alias A second name for another object's property property alias text: label.text

You'll meet each of these in later chapters. For now, property TYPE name: value is enough.

Comments#

// a line comment: ignored by QML
/* a block comment,
   can span lines */
Rectangle { width: 10 /* inline */ }

Comment generously while learning. Future you will thank you.

Imports#

The first lines of every file say which modules to load:

import QtQuick                 // Item, Rectangle, Text, Image, MouseArea, animations…
import QtQuick.Layouts         // RowLayout, ColumnLayout, GridLayout
import QtQuick.Controls        // Button, Slider, Switch, TextField…
import Quickshell              // PanelWindow, Variants, Scope, SystemClock…
import Quickshell.Io           // Process, FileView, IpcHandler…
import Quickshell.Services.UPower   // UPower, UPowerDevice…

Forget an import and you get X is not a type. In Qt 6 you don't write version numbers (old tutorials show import QtQuick 2.15; that still works but isn't needed).

Putting it together#

~/.config/quickshell/playground/shell.qmlimport Quickshell
import QtQuick

PanelWindow {
    anchors { top: true; left: true; right: true }
    implicitHeight: 40
    color: "#11111b"

    // our own state
    property int level: 65
    property string name: "Volume"

    Rectangle {                          // the track
        x: 12; y: 14
        width: 200; height: 12
        radius: 6
        color: "#313244"

        Rectangle {                      // the filled part, child of the track
            width: parent.width * level / 100
            height: parent.height
            radius: 6
            color: "#cba6f7"
        }
    }

    Text {
        x: 224; y: 11
        text: name + ": " + level + "%"
        color: "#cdd6f4"
    }
}

Change level to 20 and save. The bar shrinks and the label updates. You changed one number and two things on screen followed it. That's the next big idea, bindings, which Bindings: The Heart of QML explains properly.

Exercises
  1. Add property color accent: "#a6e3a1" to the window and use it for the filled bar's color.
  2. Add a third rectangle as a "knob" at the end of the filled part (hint: x: parent.width * level / 100 - 6).
  3. Try to set a property that doesn't exist and read the error.
Part II · The QML Language

Value Types in Depth

Every property has a type that says what kind of value it holds. Using the right type gives you better error messages, faster code and editor autocomplete. This chapter is a complete tour, with the traps beginners fall into.

Overview#

Type Holds Example literal Default
bool true or false true false
int whole number 42, -3, 0xff 0
real decimal number 3.14, 0.5, 1e3 0
double same as real 0.25 0
string text "hello", 'hi' ""
color a color "#cba6f7", "red" black / invalid
url a file or web address "icons/a.svg", "file:///…" empty
date a date and time new Date() invalid
point x, y Qt.point(10, 20) (0,0)
size width, height Qt.size(100, 50) (0,0)
rect x, y, width, height Qt.rect(0, 0, 100, 50) zero
font a font description Qt.font({ family: "Inter", pixelSize: 14 }) system font
var anything (JS value) ({ a: 1 }), [1, 2] undefined
list<T> a typed list ["a", "b"] empty
object types a reference to an object property Item target, property UPowerDevice bat null

bool#

property bool open: false
visible: open                    // an object is shown only when this is true
onOpenChanged: console.log("open is now", open)

Any expression that yields a truthy or falsy JS value converts to bool: visible: someList.length shows the item when the list isn't empty.

int and real#

property int count: 3
property real ratio: 0.75

width: 100 * ratio               // 75
Division always gives a decimal

7 / 2 is 3.5 in JavaScript, even between ints. If you assign 3.5 to an int property it's truncated to 3. Use Math.round(), Math.floor() or Math.ceil() to control rounding: Math.round(bat.percentage * 100).

Handy number methods:

text: ratio.toFixed(2)           // "0.75": a STRING with 2 decimals
text: Math.round(cpu * 100) + "%"
property real clamped: Math.max(0, Math.min(1, value))   // keep between 0 and 1

string#

property string name: "kitty"
text: "Hello " + name                       // concatenation
text: `Hello ${name}, you have ${n} items`  // template string: easiest for mixing

Common string methods (plain JavaScript):

Method Result
s.length number of characters
s.toUpperCase() / toLowerCase() case conversion
s.trim() remove whitespace at both ends (essential for command output!)
s.includes("x") contains?
s.startsWith("x") / endsWith prefix/suffix check
s.split("\n") split into an array of lines
s.slice(0, 10) first 10 characters
s.replace(/foo/g, "bar") regex replace
s.padStart(2, "0") "7" → "07"

Special characters: "\n" newline, "\t" tab, "\"" a quote, "\\" a backslash, "°" a Unicode character (°).

color#

color: "red"                    // SVG color names
color: "#cba6f7"                // #RRGGBB
color: "#80cba6f7"              // #AARRGGBB, alpha FIRST
color: Qt.rgba(1, 0.5, 0, 0.8)  // components 0.0–1.0
color: Qt.hsla(0.75, 0.6, 0.7, 1)
color: "transparent"
Alpha comes first in Qt

In CSS, #rrggbbaa puts alpha last. In QML, 8-digit hex is #aarrggbb: alpha first. "#80000000" is 50% transparent black. Mixing these up is the #1 color bug.

Color helpers:

color: Qt.lighter(base, 1.2)            // 20% lighter
color: Qt.darker(base, 1.5)
color: Qt.tint(base, "#40ffffff")        // blend a transparent overlay on top
color: Qt.alpha(base, 0.5)               // same color, 50% alpha (Qt 6.8+)
color: Qt.rgba(base.r, base.g, base.b, 0.5)   // same, works on every version

A color value has readable components: c.r, c.g, c.b, c.a (0–1), and c.hsvHue, c.hsvSaturation, c.hsvValue, c.hslHue, c.hslSaturation, c.hslLightness.

url#

source: "icons/wifi.svg"                         // relative: to THIS .qml file's folder
source: "file:///home/me/Pictures/wall.jpg"      // absolute file URL
source: "file://" + Quickshell.env("HOME") + "/.face"
source: Qt.resolvedUrl("assets/logo.png")       // make a relative path absolute
source: "image://icon/firefox"                   // icon-theme lookup (Quickshell provides this)

A relative URL resolves against the file that contains it, not the folder you ran qs from. That's handy: a component in widgets/ can say source: "icons/x.svg" and find widgets/icons/x.svg.

date#

property date now: new Date()
text: Qt.formatDateTime(now, "dddd, d MMMM yyyy · hh:mm")
text: now.getHours() + ":" + String(now.getMinutes()).padStart(2, "0")

Timers, Dates and Time covers date formatting in detail, plus SystemClock.

point, size, rect#

Small value types with named parts:

property point p: Qt.point(10, 20)          // p.x, p.y
property size s: Qt.size(300, 200)          // s.width, s.height
property rect r: Qt.rect(0, 0, 100, 50)     // r.x, r.y, r.width, r.height

Image { sourceSize: Qt.size(128, 128) }     // decode an image at 128×128

var: anything at all#

var holds any JavaScript value: objects, arrays, functions, null.

property var config: ({ height: 32, modules: ["clock", "tray"] })   // note the ( )
property var callback: (x) => console.log(x)
property var nothing: null
Wrap object literals in parentheses

property var obj: { a: 1 } is parsed as a code block, not an object, and gives undefined. Always write ({ a: 1 }).

Changes inside a var are invisible

QML notices when a property is assigned, not when something inside it changes:

property var items: []
function add(x) {
    items.push(x)          // ✗ nothing that uses `items` updates
    items = [...items, x]  // ✓ a new array is assigned, so bindings update
}

The same applies to list<T> and to objects: obj.a = 2 doesn't notify, obj = Object.assign({}, obj, { a: 2 }) does.

list<T>#

A typed list. Prefer it over var when every element has the same type:

property list<string> pinned: ["firefox", "kitty", "spotify"]
property list<int> sizes: [12, 14, 18]
property list<Item> panels               // list of objects

Use them like JS arrays: pinned.length, pinned[0], pinned.includes("kitty"), pinned.map(…). The same "assign a new list to notify" rule applies.

Object types: references to other objects#

A property can hold a reference to an object of a specific type:

import Quickshell.Services.UPower

Item {
    property UPowerDevice battery: UPower.displayDevice   // typed reference
    property Item target                                  // null until assigned
    property QtObject anything                            // any object at all
}

Typed references give you autocomplete and errors if you assign the wrong kind of object. Every Quickshell type in the API reference can be used as a property type.

null and undefined, and optional chaining#

Object references are often null, for example before a service is ready or when no media player is running. Reading a property of null throws an error:

TypeError: Cannot read property 'trackTitle' of null

Use optional chaining ?. and nullish coalescing ??:

text: Mpris.players.values[0]?.trackTitle ?? "Nothing playing"
//                             ^^ stop here if null      ^^ fallback value

You'll write ?. and ?? constantly in shells, because system state comes and goes.

Type conversion cheatsheet#

From → to How
number → string String(n), n.toString(), n.toFixed(1), `${n}`
string → int parseInt("42")
string → real parseFloat("3.5"), Number("3.5"), +"3.5"
string → bool s === "true"
anything → JSON text JSON.stringify(x)
JSON text → object JSON.parse(text)
color → string String(c) gives "#rrggbb"
Exercises
  1. Make a property real level: 0.42 and show it as 42% using Math.round.
  2. Make a semi-transparent (40%) version of #89b4fa in two ways: 8-digit hex, then Qt.rgba.
  3. Create property var apps: [] and a Timer that appends a new string every second. First use push and see nothing update. Then fix it.
Part II · The QML Language

ids, parent and Scope

Objects need to refer to each other: "make this text the same width as that box", "when this button is clicked, open that popup". QML gives you three ways to name things: ids, parent and scope lookup.

ids#

An id is a name you give an object so other objects in the same file can refer to it:

Rectangle {
    id: root
    width: 300; height: 60
    color: "#1e1e2e"

    Rectangle {
        id: knob
        width: root.height            // use another object's property
        height: root.height
        radius: height / 2
        color: "#cba6f7"
    }

    Text {
        anchors.left: knob.right      // position relative to knob
        anchors.leftMargin: 10
        anchors.verticalCenter: parent.verticalCenter
        text: "knob is " + knob.width + "px wide"
        color: "white"
    }
}

Rules:

  • id isn't a normal property: no quotes, no type, can't be changed later.
  • Must start with a lowercase letter or underscore: root, clockText, _internal.
  • Must be unique within the file.
  • Is visible everywhere in that file, at any depth, in any direction (a child can name its parent's sibling).
  • Is invisible outside the file. Another file can't see knob; you pass things between files with properties (next chapters).
Name the root root

By convention every file's root object gets id: root. Then anywhere in the file, root.someProperty clearly means "the top object of this file".

parent#

parent always refers to an item's visual parent, the object it's nested inside:

Rectangle {
    width: 200; height: 50
    Rectangle {
        width: parent.width / 2     // half of the outer rectangle
        height: parent.height
    }
}

parent is convenient for "fill my container" code (anchors.fill: parent), but it changes meaning if you move the object somewhere else. When you mean a specific object, use its id.

this#

Inside a JavaScript function or signal handler, this is the object the code belongs to. You rarely need it, since ids are clearer, but you'll see it in upstream docs, e.g. inside a StdioCollector: onStreamFinished: console.log(this.text).

How bare names are found (scope lookup)#

When you write a name without id. in front, like height or volume, QML searches in this order:

  1. JavaScript locals: function parameters, let/const variables.
  2. The current object's properties.
  3. ids in the file.
  4. The root object's properties (properties of the file's top object).
  5. The surrounding context: things like index and modelData provided by a Repeater or ListView delegate.
  6. Singletons and global names: Quickshell, Hyprland, Qt, Math, console.
Rectangle {
    id: root
    property int volume: 50       // root property

    Rectangle {
        property int volume: 10   // shadows the root's volume!
        width: volume             // → 10  (current object wins)
        height: root.volume       // → 50  (explicit)
    }
}
Be explicit

Unqualified names that reach outward (to the root or to delegate context) are a common source of confusing bugs and are slower for the engine. Prefer root.volume over volume when you mean the root's property, and declare delegate data with required property (Models, Repeater and ListView).

Talking between files: properties in, signals out#

Since ids don't cross files, components communicate through their public properties and signals:

Counter.qmlimport QtQuick

Rectangle {
    id: root
    property int value: 0          // input/state, visible to the user of Counter
    signal clicked()               // output: tells the outside something happened

    width: 60; height: 30; radius: 6
    color: "#45475a"
    Text { anchors.centerIn: parent; text: root.value; color: "white" }
    MouseArea { anchors.fill: parent; onClicked: root.clicked() }
}
shell.qmlimport Quickshell
import QtQuick

PanelWindow {
    anchors { top: true; left: true; right: true }
    implicitHeight: 40

    Counter {
        id: counter
        anchors.centerIn: parent
        onClicked: counter.value++       // the user of the component decides what a click does
    }
}

This "data down, events up" pattern keeps components reusable. You'll formalize it in Components, Files and Imports.

Global state: singletons#

For things many files need (volume, theme colors, "is the launcher open"), passing properties through every level gets tedious. QML has singletons: one global object accessible by name from any file. Quickshell provides many (Quickshell, Hyprland, UPower, Pipewire…) and you'll write your own in Singletons and Global State.

Text { text: Hyprland.focusedWorkspace?.name ?? "" }   // Hyprland is a singleton: no id needed
Exercises
  1. Make three rectangles in a row where each one's width is twice the previous one's, using ids.
  2. Reproduce the shadowing example and print both values with console.log in Component.onCompleted.
  3. Build Counter.qml and use two counters: clicking the first increments the second (hint: give them ids in shell.qml).
Part II · The QML Language

Bindings: The Heart of QML

If you understand this chapter, you understand QML. A binding is a property whose value is an expression that QML keeps up to date automatically.

The idea#

Rectangle {
    id: root
    property int volume: 40

    width: 200
    height: 20
    color: volume > 80 ? "red" : "grey"     // ← binding

    Rectangle {
        width: parent.width * root.volume / 100   // ← binding
        height: parent.height
        color: "white"
    }
}

color: volume > 80 ? "red" : "grey" isn't run once. QML:

  1. evaluates the expression,
  2. records every property it read (here: volume),
  3. re-evaluates it whenever any of those properties change.

So if anything sets volume = 90 (a click, a timer, the audio service), the color turns red and the inner bar grows, with no update code anywhere. That's why a full desktop bar in QML can have almost no "logic".

What can go in a binding#

Any JavaScript expression:

text: "Battery: " + Math.round(bat.percentage * 100) + "%"
visible: players.length > 0 && !GlobalStates.dnd
opacity: hovered ? 1.0 : 0.6
width: Math.max(label.implicitWidth + 20, 60)
color: Colors.primary

For more complex logic, use a block. The last return gives the value:

text: {
    const p = Math.round(bat.percentage * 100)
    if (bat.state === UPowerDeviceState.Charging) return "⚡ " + p + "%"
    if (p < 15) return "‼ " + p + "%"
    return p + "%"
}

Or call a function. QML tracks the properties the function reads, too:

function label(): string {
    return players.length ? players[0].trackTitle : "Idle"
}
text: label()      // re-evaluates when players or trackTitle change

Bindings vs assignments#

There are two ways to give a property a value:

Syntax Where Effect
Binding width: parent.width / 2 in the object body stays up to date forever
Assignment width = 50 inside JavaScript (handlers, functions) sets a fixed value and removes any binding 
Rectangle {
    id: box
    width: parent.width / 2               // binding

    MouseArea {
        anchors.fill: parent
        onClicked: box.width = 50          // ⚠ binding destroyed: box.width is now
                                           //   always 50, even if the parent resizes
    }
}

This is the most common "it stopped updating!" bug. Think of it like this: bindings describe what something is; assignments are for events.

Restoring a binding from JavaScript#

onClicked: box.width = Qt.binding(() => parent.width / 4)   // a NEW binding

The better pattern: bind to state, change the state#

Instead of assigning to visual properties, keep a small piece of state and bind visuals to it:

Rectangle {
    id: box
    property bool expanded: false            // state
    width: expanded ? 300 : 120              // visual, bound to state
    height: expanded ? 200 : 40
    color: expanded ? "#cba6f7" : "#45475a"

    MouseArea { anchors.fill: parent; onClicked: box.expanded = !box.expanded }  // only touch state
}

You assign only to expanded, a property no binding depends on for its own value, and everything visual stays a binding. This scales to entire shells: one GlobalStates.launcherOpen boolean drives the launcher window, the bar button highlight and the blur, all through bindings.

Binding loops#

If a property depends on itself, directly or in a circle, QML stops and warns:

Rectangle {
    width: height
    height: width + 1      // width → height → width …
}
QML Rectangle: Binding loop detected for property "width"

The fix is always to break the circle: one of the values must come from somewhere else (a constant, the parent, the content). Layout code is the usual culprit: a parent's size depends on its child and the child's size depends on the parent. Sizing and Implicit Size shows how to avoid this.

Performance notes#

  • Bindings are cheap. A bar with hundreds is fine.
  • An expensive binding (sorting 500 apps) re-runs every time any input changes. Compute it once into a readonly property and reuse it.
  • Don't read a frequently changing property (like a playback position updated every frame) in a binding that does heavy work.

The Binding object (conditional bindings)#

Sometimes you want a binding only while a condition holds:

Binding {
    target: osd
    property: "visible"
    value: true
    when: Audio.volumeChangedRecently       // while true, osd.visible = true; afterwards the old value returns
}

You'll rarely need this, but it's useful for "override while hovering" or "force while locked" situations.

A complete example: everything flows from one value#

~/.config/quickshell/playground/shell.qmlimport Quickshell
import QtQuick

PanelWindow {
    id: win
    anchors { top: true; left: true; right: true }
    implicitHeight: 44
    color: "#11111b"

    property real level: 0.3                       // the ONLY state

    Rectangle {
        id: track
        anchors { left: parent.left; leftMargin: 14; verticalCenter: parent.verticalCenter }
        width: 260; height: 14; radius: 7
        color: "#313244"

        Rectangle {
            width: track.width * win.level
            height: parent.height; radius: 7
            color: win.level > 0.8 ? "#f38ba8" : win.level > 0.5 ? "#f9e2af" : "#a6e3a1"
            Behavior on width { NumberAnimation { duration: 200 } }   // animate changes (Ch. 23)
        }
    }
    Text {
        anchors { left: track.right; leftMargin: 12; verticalCenter: parent.verticalCenter }
        text: Math.round(win.level * 100) + "%" + (win.level > 0.8 ? "  LOUD" : "")
        color: "#cdd6f4"
        font.bold: win.level > 0.8
    }
    MouseArea {                                     // scroll anywhere to change level
        anchors.fill: parent
        onWheel: w => win.level = Math.max(0, Math.min(1, win.level + (w.angleDelta.y > 0 ? 0.05 : -0.05)))
    }
}

Scroll on the bar: the fill, its color, the label and the bold text all follow level. That one assignment in onWheel is the only imperative line in the file.

Exercises
  1. In the example, add a second bar below that shows 1 - level.
  2. Break a binding on purpose: add a button that assigns the fill's width = 30, then scroll. Fix it with Qt.binding.
  3. Rewrite it so a click toggles a property bool muted, and when muted the fill is grey and the label says "muted", without assigning to any visual property.
Part II · The QML Language

Signals, Handlers and Connections

Bindings describe what things are. Signals describe what happens: a click, a timer firing, a command finishing, a notification arriving. This chapter covers how to react to them.

Signals and handlers#

A signal is an event an object announces. You react by writing a handler: on + the signal name with a capital first letter.

MouseArea {
    anchors.fill: parent
    onClicked: console.log("clicked!")       // signal: clicked → handler: onClicked
    onDoubleClicked: console.log("double!")
    onPressAndHold: console.log("long press")
}
Timer {
    interval: 1000; running: true; repeat: true
    onTriggered: console.log("tick")         // signal: triggered
}

Every type documents its signals. In this book's API reference each signal is listed with its handler name, e.g. Process has started → onStarted and exited(exitCode, exitStatus) → onExited.

Signal arguments#

Many signals carry data. Receive it by writing the handler as an arrow function (recommended) or a function:

MouseArea {
    acceptedButtons: Qt.LeftButton | Qt.RightButton
    onClicked: mouse => {                          // arrow function with a parameter
        if (mouse.button === Qt.RightButton) console.log("right click at", mouse.x, mouse.y)
    }
}

Process {
    command: ["ls"]
    onExited: (code, status) => console.log("ls finished with code", code)   // two arguments
}

You can name the parameters whatever you like; their position is what matters.

Old style

Older code accesses arguments by their declared names without listing them, like onClicked: console.log(mouse.x). This is deprecated in Qt 6 and prints a warning. Always use the arrow form.

Property change signals#

Every property automatically has a change signal named <property>Changed, so you can react to any value changing:

Rectangle {
    property int volume: 50
    onVolumeChanged: console.log("volume is now", volume)
    onWidthChanged: console.log("resized to", width)
    onVisibleChanged: if (visible) console.log("shown!")
}

This is how an OSD knows to pop up when the volume changes, no matter what changed it:

Connections {
    target: Pipewire.defaultAudioSink?.audio ?? null
    function onVolumeChanged() { osd.show() }
}

Declaring your own signals#

IconButton.qmlimport QtQuick

Rectangle {
    id: root
    signal clicked()                           // no arguments
    signal scrolled(int direction)             // one typed argument
    signal picked(string name, int index)      // several

    width: 32; height: 32; radius: 16
    color: "#45475a"
    MouseArea {
        anchors.fill: parent
        onClicked: root.clicked()                             // emit by calling it like a function
        onWheel: w => root.scrolled(w.angleDelta.y > 0 ? 1 : -1)
    }
}

Users of the component handle them like built-in signals:

IconButton {
    onClicked: console.log("button clicked")
    onScrolled: dir => volume += dir * 5
}

Component.onCompleted and onDestruction#

Every object has the attached Component signals:

Item {
    Component.onCompleted: console.log("I was created and all my properties are set")
    Component.onDestruction: console.log("I'm about to be destroyed")
}

onCompleted is the place for one-time setup. Don't overuse it for things a binding could express.

Connections: handling another object's signals#

A handler like onClicked must live inside the object that emits the signal. To react to signals of an object somewhere else, especially singletons and services, use Connections:

import Quickshell.Hyprland

Connections {
    target: Hyprland                           // whose signals
    function onRawEvent(event) {               // function form: on + SignalName
        console.log("hyprland event:", event.name, event.data)
    }
}

Connections properties:

Property Meaning
target The object to listen to. Can be a binding, so it switches automatically when the target changes.
enabled Set false to temporarily stop listening.
ignoreUnknownSignals Don't warn if the target doesn't have one of the handlers. 
Connections {
    target: Media.active            // follows whichever player is active
    enabled: target !== null
    function onTrackChanged() { coverAnim.restart() }
}

Connecting in JavaScript#

You can also connect signals to functions in code. This is rarely needed, but useful for one-off listeners:

Component.onCompleted: {
    button.clicked.connect(onButton)          // connect
    // button.clicked.disconnect(onButton)    // disconnect later
}
function onButton() { console.log("connected handler ran") }

Signals vs bindings: which to use?#

Situation Use
"X should always equal / depend on Y" binding
"When X happens, do something once" (click, finish, arrive) signal handler
"When X changes, start an animation / show a popup / run a command" change handler (onXChanged) or Connections
"Many files need to know" a singleton property they all bind to
Avoid "handler soup"

A beginner often writes onVolumeChanged: label.text = volume + "%". That's a binding written the hard way. If a handler only assigns a value derived from other properties, replace it with a binding.

Complete example#

~/.config/quickshell/playground/shell.qmlimport Quickshell
import QtQuick

PanelWindow {
    id: win
    anchors { top: true; left: true; right: true }
    implicitHeight: 40
    color: "#11111b"

    property int clicks: 0
    signal milestone(int value)

    onClicksChanged: if (clicks % 5 === 0) milestone(clicks)    // emit our own signal
    onMilestone: value => flash.restart()                        // handle it

    Rectangle {
        id: button
        anchors.centerIn: parent
        width: 160; height: 28; radius: 14
        color: area.pressed ? "#585b70" : area.containsMouse ? "#45475a" : "#313244"

        Text { anchors.centerIn: parent; color: "#cdd6f4"; text: "clicked " + win.clicks + "×" }

        MouseArea {
            id: area
            anchors.fill: parent
            hoverEnabled: true
            acceptedButtons: Qt.LeftButton | Qt.RightButton
            onClicked: m => win.clicks += (m.button === Qt.RightButton ? -1 : 1)
        }

        SequentialAnimation on scale {         // plays when we call flash.restart()
            id: flash
            running: false
            NumberAnimation { to: 1.25; duration: 120 }
            NumberAnimation { to: 1.0; duration: 200; easing.type: Easing.OutBack }
        }
    }
}
Exercises
  1. Add a Timer that resets clicks to 0 if you don't click for 3 seconds (hint: restart() it in onClicked).
  2. Create Toggle.qml with property bool checked and signal toggled(bool checked), and use it in the bar.
  3. Use Connections to log every time the window's width changes (target: win).
Part II · The QML Language

The JavaScript You Need

Every expression in QML is JavaScript. You don't need to learn all of JavaScript, just the part that shows up in shells: variables, conditions, strings, arrays, objects, functions, JSON, dates and math. This chapter teaches that subset from zero.

Where JavaScript appears#

Item {
    width: 100 * 2                                  // 1. binding expressions
    onWidthChanged: console.log(width)              // 2. signal handlers
    function double(x) { return x * 2 }             // 3. functions
    Component.onCompleted: {                        // 4. multi-line blocks
        const list = [1, 2, 3]
        console.log(list.map(double))
    }
}

Variables#

const name = "kitty"        // can't be reassigned: use by default
let count = 0               // can be reassigned
count = count + 1
count += 1                  // same thing
count++                     // same thing
// var x = 1                // old style: avoid

Variables declared inside a handler or function exist only there. To remember a value between events, use a QML property.

Conditions#

if (pct < 15) {
    color = "red"
} else if (pct < 40) {
    color = "orange"
} else {
    color = "green"
}

// ternary: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse (perfect for bindings)
text: charging ? "charging" : "on battery"

// comparisons: === equal, !== not equal, <, >, <=, >=
// logic: && and, || or, ! not
visible: hasBattery && !hidden
Use === not ==

== converts types in surprising ways ("0" == 0 is true). Always use === and !==.

Truthy and falsy#

These count as false: false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is true, including "0", [] and {}. So if (title) means "if title is non-empty".

?? and ?.#

const t = player?.trackTitle ?? "Nothing playing"   // see Chapter 7
const n = count || 1     // || falls back on ANY falsy value (also 0!)
const m = count ?? 1     // ?? falls back only on null/undefined (keeps 0)

switch#

switch (state) {
case "charging": icon = "battery_charging_full"; break
case "full":     icon = "battery_full"; break
default:         icon = "battery_5_bar"
}

Strings#

const s = "  Hello World  "
s.trim()                    // "Hello World"
s.toLowerCase()             // "  hello world  "
s.includes("World")         // true
s.split(" ")                // ["", "", "Hello", "World", "", ""]
s.trim().split(/\s+/)       // ["Hello", "World"]: split on any whitespace
"a,b,c".split(",")          // ["a", "b", "c"]
["a", "b"].join(" · ")      // "a · b"
"abc".slice(1)              // "bc"
"7".padStart(2, "0")        // "07"
`CPU ${Math.round(cpu)}%`   // template string

Regular expressions#

Patterns for matching text, which is very useful for parsing command output:

const line = "MemAvailable:    8123456 kB"
const m = line.match(/MemAvailable:\s+(\d+)/)   // ( ) captures a group
const kb = m ? parseInt(m[1]) : 0                // m[1] is the first captured group

"wifi_1_bar".replace(/_\d_bar/, "")              // "wifi"
/^\d+$/.test("123")                              // true: is it all digits?

Cheat sheet: \d digit, \s whitespace, \w word char, . any char, + one or more, * zero or more, ? optional, ^ start, $ end, (…) capture, [abc] one of, g flag = all matches, i flag = ignore case.

Arrays#

const apps = ["firefox", "kitty", "spotify"]
apps.length                 // 3
apps[0]                     // "firefox"
apps[apps.length - 1]       // "spotify"
apps.includes("kitty")      // true
apps.indexOf("kitty")       // 1 (-1 if missing)

The big four: map, filter, find, sort#

These are what you'll use most, to turn system data into what you display:

const nums = [5, 1, 4]
nums.map(n => n * 2)                  // [10, 2, 8]: transform every element
nums.filter(n => n > 2)               // [5, 4]: keep matching elements
nums.find(n => n > 2)                 // 5: first match (undefined if none)
nums.some(n => n > 4)                 // true: does any match?
nums.every(n => n > 0)                // true: do all match?
[...nums].sort((a, b) => a - b)       // [1, 4, 5]: sort a COPY numerically
nums.reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0)   // 10: combine into one value
sort() changes the array in place

arr.sort() modifies arr, and on a QML list that can confuse bindings. Sort a copy: [...arr].sort(…). Also note sort() without a function sorts as strings ([10, 9, 1] becomes [1, 10, 9]).

Real example: the active media player, or the first one:

readonly property var active: Mpris.players.values.find(p => p.isPlaying) ?? Mpris.players.values[0] ?? null

Real example: apps matching a search, best match first:

DesktopEntries.applications.values
    .filter(a => a.name.toLowerCase().includes(query.toLowerCase()))
    .sort((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name))
    .slice(0, 20)

Building new arrays#

const more = [...apps, "discord"]            // add (new array: notifies QML!)
const fewer = apps.filter(a => a !== "kitty") // remove
const copy = [...apps]
for (const app of apps) console.log(app)     // loop over values
apps.forEach((app, i) => console.log(i, app))

Objects#

const bat = { pct: 80, charging: true }
bat.pct                      // 80
bat["charging"]              // true
bat.health = 95              // add a key
Object.keys(bat)             // ["pct", "charging", "health"]
Object.entries(bat)          // [["pct", 80], ...]
const { pct, charging } = bat          // destructuring
const updated = { ...bat, pct: 81 }    // copy with a change

Functions#

function add(a, b) { return a + b }                 // declaration
const add2 = (a, b) => a + b                        // arrow function (short)
const square = x => x * x                           // one param: parens optional
const fmt = (sec) => {                              // multi-line arrow
    const m = Math.floor(sec / 60)
    return `${m}:${String(sec % 60).padStart(2, "0")}`
}

In QML you can add type annotations. They're optional but catch mistakes, and they're required for IpcHandler functions:

function formatTime(seconds: int): string {
    const m = Math.floor(seconds / 60), s = seconds % 60
    return `${m}:${String(s).padStart(2, "0")}`
}

JSON#

Many commands output JSON (hyprctl -j, niri msg -j, curl APIs). Parse it into objects:

const data = JSON.parse('{"temp": 21.5, "city": "Kochi"}')
data.temp                         // 21.5
JSON.stringify(data)              // back to text
JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)     // pretty-printed, great for console.log debugging

Wrap parsing in try/catch, because malformed output would otherwise throw:

try {
    root.weather = JSON.parse(text)
} catch (e) {
    console.warn("bad weather json:", e)
}

Math#

Math.round(2.5)   // 3        Math.floor(2.9) // 2      Math.ceil(2.1) // 3
Math.max(1, 5)    // 5        Math.min(1, 5)  // 1      Math.abs(-3)   // 3
Math.random()     // 0..1     Math.PI                   Math.sin(x)
Math.pow(2, 8)    // 256      2 ** 8          // 256    Math.sqrt(16)  // 4
const clamp = (v, lo, hi) => Math.max(lo, Math.min(hi, v))

Dates#

const now = new Date()
now.getHours(); now.getMinutes(); now.getDay()   // 0 = Sunday
now.getFullYear(); now.getMonth()                // month is 0-based! (0 = January)
new Date(2026, 0, 1)                             // 1 Jan 2026
Date.now()                                       // milliseconds since 1970 (for timing)

For display, use Qt's formatter: Qt.formatDateTime(now, "ddd d MMM hh:mm") (Timers, Dates and Time).

Shared JavaScript files#

Put reusable helpers in a .js file and import it:

utils/format.js.pragma library          // load once and share between all files (no access to QML ids)

function bytes(b) {
    const u = ["B", "KiB", "MiB", "GiB", "TiB"]
    let i = 0
    while (b >= 1024 && i < u.length - 1) { b /= 1024; i++ }
    return b.toFixed(i ? 1 : 0) + " " + u[i]
}

function duration(sec) {
    const h = Math.floor(sec / 3600), m = Math.floor((sec % 3600) / 60)
    return h ? `${h}h ${m}m` : `${m}m`
}
import "utils/format.js" as Format

Text { text: Format.bytes(1536000) }      // "1.5 MiB"
In the wild

end-4 bundles libraries like fuzzysort.js for launcher search this way, and keeps string and color helpers in .js files.

Debugging JavaScript#

console.log("value:", x)                    // print
console.log(JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2))   // print an object readably
console.warn("something odd")               // yellow
console.error("broken")                     // red
console.trace()                             // print the call stack
console.time("sort"); /* … */ console.timeEnd("sort")   // measure duration
Exercises
  1. Write function plural(n, word) that returns "1 item" / "3 items".
  2. Given const lines = ["a:1", "b:22", "c:3"], build {a: 1, b: 22, c: 3} with map, split and Object.fromEntries.
  3. Parse "MemTotal: 16000000 kB\nMemAvailable: 9000000 kB" with regexes and compute the used percentage.
  4. Put your plural function in utils/text.js with .pragma library and use it from QML.
Part II · The QML Language

Components, Files and Imports

A rice is made of dozens of reusable pieces: buttons, pills, icons, cards, sliders. In QML, every file is a reusable type. This chapter teaches you to build your own components with clean APIs, the way big shells do.

One file = one type#

Create a file whose name starts with a capital letter:

~/.config/quickshell/playground/Pill.qmlimport QtQuick

Rectangle {
    implicitWidth: 80
    implicitHeight: 26
    radius: height / 2
    color: "#cba6f7"
}

Now Pill is a type that any other file in the same folder can use:

~/.config/quickshell/playground/shell.qmlimport Quickshell
import QtQuick

PanelWindow {
    anchors { top: true; left: true; right: true }
    implicitHeight: 40
    Row {
        anchors.centerIn: parent
        spacing: 8
        Pill {}
        Pill {}
        Pill { color: "#a6e3a1" }       // override a property of the root object
    }
}

The type name is the filename without .qml. The file's root object (here a Rectangle) is what you get, so users can set any Rectangle property on a Pill.

Giving your component an API#

A good component exposes a few properties (inputs) and signals (outputs) and hides everything else:

Pill.qmlimport QtQuick

Rectangle {
    id: root

    // ---- public API ----
    property string text: ""
    property string icon: ""
    property color accent: "#cba6f7"
    property bool active: false
    signal clicked()
    signal rightClicked()

    // ---- implementation ----
    implicitWidth: row.implicitWidth + 20
    implicitHeight: 28
    radius: height / 2
    color: active ? accent : mouse.containsMouse ? "#45475a" : "#313244"
    Behavior on color { ColorAnimation { duration: 150 } }

    Row {
        id: row
        anchors.centerIn: parent
        spacing: 6
        Text {
            visible: root.icon !== ""
            text: root.icon
            font.family: "Material Symbols Rounded"
            font.pixelSize: 16
            color: root.active ? "#1e1e2e" : "#cdd6f4"
        }
        Text {
            text: root.text
            color: root.active ? "#1e1e2e" : "#cdd6f4"
            font.pixelSize: 13
        }
    }

    MouseArea {
        id: mouse
        anchors.fill: parent
        hoverEnabled: true
        acceptedButtons: Qt.LeftButton | Qt.RightButton
        cursorShape: Qt.PointingHandCursor
        onClicked: m => m.button === Qt.RightButton ? root.rightClicked() : root.clicked()
    }
}
Pill { icon: "wifi"; text: "Home-5G"; active: true }
Pill { icon: "bluetooth"; text: "Off"; onClicked: console.log("toggle bt") }

property alias: exposing an inner property#

An alias makes an inner object's property available as if it were the component's own:

Label.qmlimport QtQuick

Rectangle {
    property alias text: inner.text          // Label.text IS inner.text
    property alias textColor: inner.color
    property alias font: inner.font          // expose the whole font group

    implicitWidth: inner.implicitWidth + 16
    implicitHeight: inner.implicitHeight + 8
    radius: 6
    color: "#313244"
    Text { id: inner; anchors.centerIn: parent; color: "white" }
}
Label { text: "hello"; font.bold: true; textColor: "#f9e2af" }

Aliases are two-way: setting Label.text sets inner.text and vice versa.

required properties#

Mark a property required when the component can't work without it. Forgetting it becomes an error instead of a silent bug:

WorkspaceDot.qmlimport QtQuick

Rectangle {
    required property int workspaceId
    required property bool active
    width: active ? 24 : 8; height: 8; radius: 4
    color: active ? "#cba6f7" : "#585b70"
}
WorkspaceDot { workspaceId: 3; active: true }   // OK
WorkspaceDot { }                                // ERROR: Required property workspaceId was not initialized

required is also how delegates receive their data in Repeaters and ListViews (Models, Repeater and ListView).

default property: components that take children#

To let users put children inside your component and have them land in the right place, use a default property:

Card.qmlimport QtQuick

Rectangle {
    default property alias content: column.data   // children go into the column
    property string title: ""

    implicitWidth: 260
    implicitHeight: column.implicitHeight + 24
    radius: 14
    color: "#1e1e2e"
    border.color: "#313244"

    Column {
        id: column
        anchors { left: parent.left; right: parent.right; top: parent.top; margins: 12 }
        spacing: 6
        Text { text: title; color: "#cba6f7"; font.bold: true; visible: title !== "" }
    }
}
Card {
    title: "System"
    Text { text: "CPU 12%"; color: "white" }      // these go into Card's column
    Text { text: "RAM 41%"; color: "white" }
}

Inline components#

For a small type used only inside one file, declare it inline with component:

Item {
    component Badge: Rectangle {
        property string label
        width: 22; height: 22; radius: 11
        color: "#f38ba8"
        Text { anchors.centerIn: parent; text: parent.label; color: "white"; font.pixelSize: 11 }
    }

    Row {
        spacing: 4
        Badge { label: "3" }
        Badge { label: "9+" }
    }
}

Imports: using components from other folders#

Files in the same folder see each other automatically. For other folders:

import "widgets"              // relative path: every Capitalized.qml in ./widgets
import "../common"            // up one level
import "widgets" as W         // namespaced: write W.Pill { }

The qs import root (recommended)#

Quickshell defines a module called qs that points at your config's root folder. Use it to import any folder with an absolute-style path that works from any depth:

~/.config/quickshell/myshell/
├── shell.qml
├── services/Audio.qml
├── widgets/Pill.qml
└── modules/bar/Bar.qml
modules/bar/Bar.qmlimport qs.widgets          // → myshell/widgets/   (Pill)
import qs.services         // → myshell/services/  (Audio)

No ../../ chains, and moving a file doesn't break its imports. This is what modern rices use.

Folder names must be valid identifiers for qs. imports

qs.modules.bar works. A folder called my-widgets can't be written as qs.my-widgets, so use myWidgets or my_widgets. Relative string imports (import "my-widgets") have no such restriction.

How the root object type affects your component#

Your component is its root object, plus whatever you added:

  • Root Item: an invisible container with your API, the most flexible.
  • Root Rectangle: users can set color, radius and so on.
  • Root MouseArea: the whole component is clickable.
