  • Root PanelWindow: your component is a window (e.g. Bar.qml).
  • Root Scope: a non-visual group that can contain several windows (Shell Structure, Pragmas and Reloading).

Choose the root carefully, because it's part of your public API: if Pill's root is a Rectangle, someone can override color and break your styling. Wrap it in an Item root if you want to hide that.

Designing good components#

  1. Size yourself from your content with implicitWidth/implicitHeight (Sizing and Implicit Size); never hard-code width/height on your root.
  2. Expose state, not internals. property bool active beats property color backgroundColor.
  3. Signals for events. Let the user decide what a click does.
  4. Read colors and sizes from a theme singleton (Building a Design System) instead of hard-coding them.
  5. One responsibility per file. If a file passes ~200 lines, split it.
Exercises
  1. Build IconButton.qml with properties icon (Material Symbols name), size, toggled, and signals clicked/rightClicked. Use it three times in your bar.
  2. Build Card.qml with a default property and put two Pills inside a card.
  3. Move your components into widgets/ and import them with import qs.widgets (create .qmlls.ini and restart qs so your editor understands it).
Part II · The QML Language

Attached, Grouped and Enum Properties

Three bits of syntax look odd at first: anchors.fill, Layout.fillWidth and Text.AlignHCenter. They're grouped properties, attached properties and enums. Once you can tell them apart, upstream docs and other people's rices become easy to read.

Grouped properties#

Some properties are groups of related sub-properties, written with a dot:

Text {
    font.family: "Inter"
    font.pixelSize: 14
    font.bold: true
    anchors.left: parent.left
    anchors.leftMargin: 10
}

Or in block form, same meaning:

Text {
    font { family: "Inter"; pixelSize: 14; bold: true }
    anchors { left: parent.left; leftMargin: 10 }
}

Common groups:

Group On Members
anchors Items left right top bottom horizontalCenter verticalCenter baseline fill centerIn margins leftMargin …
font Text, TextInput… family pixelSize pointSize bold weight italic letterSpacing capitalization variableAxes …
border Rectangle width color pixelAligned
anchors Quickshell PanelWindow top bottom left right (booleans: which screen edges)
margins Quickshell PanelWindow top bottom left right
easing animations type amplitude overshoot period bezierCurve
layer Items enabled smooth samples effect …

Attached properties#

An attached property is set on an object but belongs to another type. It's written TypeName.property:

RowLayout {
    Rectangle {
        Layout.fillWidth: true          // the RowLayout reads this from its child
        Layout.preferredHeight: 30
    }
}

Rectangle has no fillWidth. The Layout type attaches that property to every item so the parent layout can ask "how do you want to be sized?".

Attached properties you'll use:

Attached Purpose Example
Layout.* Size hints inside RowLayout/ColumnLayout/GridLayout Layout.fillWidth: true
Keys.* Keyboard handlers Keys.onEscapePressed: close()
Component.* Lifecycle signals Component.onCompleted: init()
ListView.* Info about a delegate inside a ListView ListView.isCurrentItem
Drag.* Make an item draggable data Drag.active: dragArea.drag.active
ToolTip.* Quick tooltip on Controls ToolTip.text: "Wi-Fi"
WlrLayershell.* Layer-shell settings on a Quickshell window WlrLayershell.layer: WlrLayer.Overlay
QsWindow.* Which window an item is in QsWindow.window
HyprlandWindow.* Hyprland-specific window settings HyprlandWindow.opacity: 0.9

Attached signals work the same way: Keys.onPressed: e => …, Component.onDestruction: ….

Reading attached values

You can read attached properties too. Inside a ListView delegate, ListView.isCurrentItem tells you if this delegate is selected. Inside any item in a Quickshell window, QsWindow.window gives you the window, which is handy for opening popups relative to it.

Enums#

An enum is a named set of fixed values, written TypeName.ValueName:

Text {
    horizontalAlignment: Text.AlignHCenter     // enum value defined on Text
    elide: Text.ElideRight
    wrapMode: Text.WordWrap
}
Image { fillMode: Image.PreserveAspectCrop }
NumberAnimation { easing.type: Easing.OutCubic }
MouseArea { cursorShape: Qt.PointingHandCursor; acceptedButtons: Qt.LeftButton | Qt.RightButton }

Under the hood an enum value is just a number, but always use the name. It's readable and survives version changes.

Quickshell's enums#

Quickshell puts enums on small dedicated types, which have their own pages in the API reference:

import Quickshell.Services.UPower
import Quickshell.Wayland

visible: bat.state === UPowerDeviceState.Charging
WlrLayershell.layer: WlrLayer.Overlay
WlrLayershell.keyboardFocus: WlrKeyboardFocus.Exclusive
exclusionMode: ExclusionMode.Ignore
anchor.edges: Edges.Bottom | Edges.Left      // flags: combine with |

Many Quickshell enum types also have a toString() function for display:

Text { text: UPowerDeviceState.toString(bat.state) }   // "Charging"
Text { text: PowerProfile.toString(PowerProfiles.profile) }

Flags: combining enum values#

Some enums are flags that can be combined with | (bitwise OR) and tested with &:

acceptedButtons: Qt.LeftButton | Qt.RightButton
onClicked: m => { if (m.modifiers & Qt.ControlModifier) console.log("ctrl-click") }
anchor.edges: Edges.Top | Edges.Right

Your own enums#

Declare enums in your own components (enum and value names start with a capital):

Bar.qmlimport QtQuick

Item {
    enum Position { Top, Bottom, Left, Right }
    property int position: Bar.Top          // refer to it through the file's type name
}

Telling them apart#

You see It's a Because
font.bold: true grouped property lowercase first part, a property of this object
Layout.fillWidth: true attached property capitalized first part, and you're setting it
Text.AlignHCenter enum value capitalized type + capitalized value, used as a value
Keys.onPressed: attached signal handler capitalized type + on…
Hyprland.focusedMonitor singleton property capitalized name that is a singleton
Exercises
  1. In a RowLayout, make three rectangles where the middle one fills the leftover width (Layout.fillWidth) and the others are 40 px wide.
  2. Set a Text's elide to Text.ElideMiddle with a narrow width and a long string.
  3. Make a MouseArea that logs "shift+click" only when Shift is held.
Part II · The QML Language

Object Lifecycle and Dynamic Creation

So far every object existed from the moment the file loaded. Real shells create things on demand: a popup when it opens, one delegate per notification, a settings page when you visit it. This chapter explains when objects are born and die, and the tools for controlling that.

Lifecycle of an object#

  1. Created: the object is constructed and its properties get default values.
  2. Properties assigned: your values and bindings are applied, in no guaranteed order.
  3. Component.onCompleted runs once everything in the file is set up.
  4. Lives: bindings update, signals fire.
  5. Component.onDestruction runs just before it's destroyed.
  6. Destroyed: its memory is freed and references to it become null.
Don't rely on property order

Within one object, QML doesn't promise which property is assigned first. Never write code in a property's change handler that assumes another property is already set during creation. Use bindings, or do setup in Component.onCompleted.

Component: a blueprint, not an object#

A Component is a description of an object that can be instantiated later, possibly many times:

Component {
    id: dotBlueprint
    Rectangle { width: 10; height: 10; radius: 5; color: "#cba6f7" }
}

Nothing is created yet. Many types take components: Loader.sourceComponent, Repeater.delegate, ListView.delegate, LazyLoader, Variants. When you write

Repeater { model: 5; Rectangle { … } }

the Rectangle { … } is implicitly wrapped in a Component and stamped out five times.

Loader: create and destroy on demand#

Loader creates an object from a component while active is true and destroys it when false:

Item {
    property bool showDetails: false

    Loader {
        id: details
        active: parent.showDetails           // false → destroyed, memory freed
        asynchronous: true                   // build without freezing the UI
        sourceComponent: Rectangle {         // inline component
            width: 300; height: 200; color: "#1e1e2e"
        }
        // or: source: "DetailsPanel.qml"
        onLoaded: console.log("created", item)   // item = the created object
    }
}
Loader property Meaning
active Whether the object should exist
sourceComponent / source What to create (inline component or a file URL)
item The created object (null while inactive)
status Loader.Null, Loading, Ready, Error
asynchronous Create in the background
progress 0–1 while loading asynchronously

Size: a Loader takes the size of its item unless you size the Loader, in which case the item is resized to fit.

Accessing the inner object's properties: details.item.someProperty, but guard against null: details.item?.someProperty.

Loader vs visible

visible: false keeps the object alive, using memory, with its timers and bindings still running. Loader { active: false } removes it entirely. For big, rarely shown UI (settings pages, the overview, the launcher), use a Loader. For small things that toggle often, visible is fine.

For whole windows, Quickshell has its own LazyLoader, covered in Lazy Loading and Memory.

Repeater and views create and destroy too#

A Repeater creates one delegate per model entry and destroys delegates when entries disappear. A ListView goes further and only creates delegates that are visible on screen. That's why a delegate must never store important state itself: it may be destroyed when it scrolls away. Keep state in the model or in a singleton.

Creating objects from JavaScript#

Rarely needed in shells, but good to know:

Item {
    id: container
    Component { id: toastComp; Rectangle { property string msg; width: 200; height: 40; color: "#313244"
        Text { anchors.centerIn: parent; text: parent.msg; color: "white" } } }

    function toast(msg) {
        const obj = toastComp.createObject(container, { msg: msg, y: 50 })   // parent + initial props
        destroyLater.createObject(container, { target: obj })
    }
    Component { id: destroyLater; Timer { property var target; interval: 2000; running: true
        onTriggered: { target.destroy(); destroy() } } }
}
  • component.createObject(parent, { props }) creates an instance.
  • obj.destroy() (or destroy(ms)) removes it.
  • Qt.createComponent("File.qml") loads a component from a file.

Prefer Loader, Repeater and models over manual creation: they clean up after themselves.

Objects and hot reload#

When you save, Quickshell reloads your config: old objects are destroyed and new ones created. That means:

  • Plain property values reset to their defaults on every reload.
  • To keep a value across reloads (e.g. "sidebar is open"), use PersistentProperties.
  • To keep a value across restarts, save it to a file with FileView + JsonAdapter (Files, Watching and JSON Config).
  • Some Quickshell objects reuse their underlying resources across reloads to avoid flicker. Windows, for example, are reused when possible, and NotificationServer can keep notifications with keepOnReload.

Quickshell signals reload events on the Quickshell singleton: reloadCompleted and reloadFailed(error).

Exercises
  1. Make a button that toggles a Loader showing a big rectangle. Add Component.onCompleted and Component.onDestruction logs inside the rectangle and watch them fire.
  2. Do the same with visible instead and notice that no logs fire after the first creation.
  3. Write a toast("hi") function like the one above and call it from a click.
Part III · Qt Quick: Drawing Things

Item and the Visual Tree

Every visible thing in Qt Quick (rectangles, text, images, your components, even the content of a Quickshell window) is an Item or inherits from it. Learn Item's properties once and you know half of every other visual type.

Item: the invisible base#

Item {
    x: 10; y: 20                // position relative to the parent's top-left corner
    width: 100; height: 50      // size
    z: 1                        // stacking order among siblings (higher = on top)
    visible: true               // false hides it AND its children; also stops input
    opacity: 1.0                // 0.0 transparent … 1.0 opaque (children too)
    enabled: true               // false disables input for it and its children
    clip: false                 // true cuts off children drawn outside its bounds
    scale: 1.0                  // grow/shrink around transformOrigin
    rotation: 0                 // degrees, clockwise
    transformOrigin: Item.Center
}

An Item draws nothing itself. It's a container and positioning helper. Use it to group things, as an invisible spacer, or as the root of components that shouldn't expose Rectangle properties.

Complete Item property reference (the ones you'll use)#

Property Type Meaning
x, y real Position relative to the parent
width, height real Actual size
implicitWidth, implicitHeight real Preferred size from content (Sizing and Implicit Size)
z real Stacking order among siblings
visible bool Shown? (inherited: a hidden parent hides children)
opacity real 0–1 transparency (multiplies down the tree)
enabled bool Accepts input?
clip bool Clip children to own rectangle
scale, rotation, transformOrigin Simple transforms
transform list Advanced transforms: Scale, Rotation, Translate, Matrix4x4
anchors.* group Attach edges to other items (Anchors)
parent Item Visual parent
children, data list Child items / all child objects
childrenRect rect Bounding box of all children
focus, activeFocus bool Keyboard focus (Mouse, Touchpad and Keyboard Input)
states, transitions, state State machine (Animation II: States, Transitions, Sequences)
layer.enabled, layer.effect Render offscreen for effects (Effects: Shadows, Blur, Masks, Tints)
antialiasing, smooth bool Edge and scaling quality
containmentMask object Custom shape for mouse hit-testing
visibleChildren list Children currently visible

Methods you might use: mapToItem(item, x, y), mapFromItem(item, x, y), mapToGlobal(x, y), contains(point), forceActiveFocus(), childAt(x, y), grabToImage(callback).

Coordinates#

Every item has its own coordinate system with (0, 0) at its top-left:

To convert between coordinate systems (e.g. "where is this button on screen, so I can open a popup there?"), use mapToItem / mapFromItem, or in Quickshell the window helpers QsWindow.itemPosition() and QsWindow.itemRect().

Stacking order: who's on top#

  1. Children draw above their parent.
  2. Later siblings draw above earlier siblings.
  3. z overrides this among siblings only: a child can't escape its parent's stacking position.
Item {
    Rectangle { color: "red";  width: 100; height: 100 }
    Rectangle { color: "blue"; width: 100; height: 100; x: 50 }        // on top of red
    Rectangle { color: "green"; width: 100; height: 100; x: 25; z: -1 } // below both
}

visible vs opacity vs enabled#

Drawn Takes space in layouts Gets mouse/keys Bindings run
visible: false no no (layouts skip it) no yes
opacity: 0 no (invisible) yes yes! yes
enabled: false yes yes no yes
Loader { active: false } no no no no (doesn't exist)
Invisible but clickable

An item with opacity: 0 still catches clicks. When fading something out, either also set visible: false at the end of the animation or disable its MouseArea.

clip#

By default children can draw outside their parent. Set clip: true to cut them off at the parent's rectangle. This is needed for scrolling lists and sliding panels:

Rectangle {
    width: 200; height: 40; radius: 8; color: "#313244"
    clip: true                                  // the long text is cut at the edge
    Text { x: 8; text: "A very very very long song title that keeps going"; color: "white" }
}

clip cuts to a rectangle and ignores radius. For rounded clipping use Quickshell's ClippingRectangle (Effects: Shadows, Blur, Masks, Tints).

Transforms#

Rectangle {
    width: 40; height: 40; color: "#cba6f7"
    rotation: 45                                 // diamond
    scale: hovered ? 1.15 : 1.0                  // grow on hover
    transformOrigin: Item.Center                 // pivot point (Center, TopLeft, Bottom…)
    property bool hovered: hh.hovered
    HoverHandler { id: hh }
}

Image {
    transform: [
        Scale { xScale: -1; origin.x: width / 2 },     // mirror horizontally
        Translate { y: 4 }
    ]
}

The visual tree vs the object tree#

Not every object is visual. Timer, Process, Connections and SystemClock have no position. They can live inside items (QML puts them in the data list) but don't draw. Quickshell's Scope and ShellRoot are non-visual containers for windows and services.

Item {
    Rectangle { }        // visual child → goes into children
    Timer { }            // non-visual → goes into data but not children
}

Inside a Quickshell window#

A PanelWindow isn't an Item itself. It's a window that contains an Item tree. Children you write inside it go into its contentItem, which fills the window. So anchors.fill: parent on a window's child means "fill the window".

Exercises
  1. Stack three overlapping circles (radius: width/2) and make the middle one come to the front when hovered (z).
  2. Make an item that fades to opacity: 0.3 when enabled is false.
  3. Rotate a Material Symbols refresh icon continuously while a property bool busy is true (hint: RotationAnimation on rotation { running: busy; loops: Animation.Infinite; from: 0; to: 360; duration: 1000 }).
Part III · Qt Quick: Drawing Things

Rectangle, Text and Image

Ninety percent of what you see in any rice is rectangles, text and images. This chapter covers each in depth: every property worth knowing and the tricks rices use.

Rectangle#

Rectangle {
    width: 240; height: 80
    color: "#1e1e2e"                  // fill
    radius: 16                        // rounded corners (height/2 = pill shape)
    border.width: 1
    border.color: "#45475a"
    antialiasing: true                // smooth edges (on by default when radius > 0)
}

Per-corner radius (Qt 6.7+)#

Rectangle {
    radius: 16                 // default for all corners
    topLeftRadius: 0           // square top-left: a "tab" attached to the left edge
    bottomLeftRadius: 0
}

Gradients#

Rectangle {
    width: 300; height: 60; radius: 12
    gradient: Gradient {
        orientation: Gradient.Horizontal          // or Vertical (default)
        GradientStop { position: 0.0; color: "#89b4fa" }
        GradientStop { position: 0.5; color: "#cba6f7" }
        GradientStop { position: 1.0; color: "#f5c2e7" }
    }
}

Built-in preset gradients exist too: gradient: Gradient.NightFade.

Shapes you can make with a Rectangle#

Shape How
Pill radius: height / 2
Circle width: height; radius: width / 2
Line / divider width: 1; height: 20 (or vice versa)
Outline only color: "transparent"; border.width: 2
Dot indicator width: 6; height: 6; radius: 3
Squircle-ish radius: width * 0.3

Rectangle properties#

Property Type Meaning
color color Fill color
radius real Corner radius for all corners
topLeftRadius topRightRadius bottomLeftRadius bottomRightRadius real Per-corner (Qt 6.7+)
border.width, border.color real, color Outline (drawn inside the rectangle)
border.pixelAligned bool Snap the border to pixels for crispness
gradient Gradient Overrides color
antialiasing bool Smooth curved edges

Text#

Text {
    text: "Hello world"
    color: "#cdd6f4"
    font.family: "Inter"
    font.pixelSize: 14               // use pixelSize for predictable sizes in shells
    font.weight: Font.DemiBold       // Thin, Light, Normal, Medium, DemiBold, Bold, Black…
    font.italic: false
    font.letterSpacing: 0.5
    font.capitalization: Font.AllUppercase
}

Fitting text into space#

Text {
    width: 200
    text: "A very long song title that will not fit in two hundred pixels"
    elide: Text.ElideRight           // "A very long song title th…"
    // elide: Text.ElideMiddle       // "A very long…two hundred pixels"
    maximumLineCount: 1
}

Text {
    width: 260
    text: "A longer body of text, such as the body of a notification, that should wrap."
    wrapMode: Text.Wrap              // NoWrap, WordWrap, WrapAnywhere, Wrap
    maximumLineCount: 3
    elide: Text.ElideRight           // "…" after the last allowed line
    lineHeight: 1.2
}

elide only works when the Text has a width limit (set width, anchors on both sides, or Layout.maximumWidth).

Alignment#

Text {
    width: 200; height: 40
    horizontalAlignment: Text.AlignHCenter     // AlignLeft, AlignRight, AlignHCenter, AlignJustify
    verticalAlignment: Text.AlignVCenter       // AlignTop, AlignBottom, AlignVCenter
}

Alignment positions the text inside the Text item's box. If the item is exactly as big as its text (the default), alignment does nothing visible; center the item with anchors instead.

Rich text#

Text {
    textFormat: Text.StyledText      // a safe, fast subset of HTML
    text: "<b>Bold</b>, <i>italic</i>, <font color='#f38ba8'>red</font>, <a href='https://x.org'>link</a>"
    onLinkActivated: link => Qt.openUrlExternally(link)
}

Formats: Text.PlainText, Text.StyledText (recommended for notification bodies), Text.RichText (fuller HTML, slower), Text.MarkdownText, Text.AutoText (guesses; avoid for untrusted input).

Readable sizes#

  • implicitWidth / implicitHeight: the size of the laid-out text.
  • contentWidth / contentHeight: the same after wrapping.
  • lineCount, truncated (true when elided).

Text properties you'll use#

Property Meaning
text, color Content and color
font.* family pixelSize pointSize weight bold italic letterSpacing wordSpacing capitalization hintingPreference variableAxes features
elide, wrapMode, maximumLineCount, lineHeight Fitting
horizontalAlignment, verticalAlignment Placement in the box
textFormat, onLinkActivated, linkColor Rich text
style, styleColor Text.Outline, Text.Raised, Text.Sunken for cheap outlines
renderType Text.QtRendering (default) or Text.NativeRendering (hinted, crisp at small sizes)
fontSizeMode, minimumPixelSize Auto-shrink to fit (Text.Fit, HorizontalFit)
padding, leftPadding… Space around the text
Crisp small text

Bar text at 11–13 px can look blurry with default rendering. Try renderType: Text.NativeRendering, or enable it globally with the //@ pragma NativeTextRendering pragma (Shell Structure, Pragmas and Reloading).

Image#

Image {
    width: 64; height: 64
    source: "file:///home/me/Pictures/cover.png"
    fillMode: Image.PreserveAspectCrop    // fill the box, crop the overflow
    sourceSize: Qt.size(128, 128)         // DECODE at this size (saves memory)
    asynchronous: true                    // load on a background thread
    smooth: true                          // smooth scaling
    mipmap: true                          // better quality when shrinking a lot
    cache: true                           // reuse decoded images (false for changing files)
}

fillMode#

Value Result
Image.Stretch (default) Stretch to the box, distorting
Image.PreserveAspectFit Fit entirely inside, letterboxed
Image.PreserveAspectCrop Fill the box, crop overflow (wallpapers, album art)
Image.Tile Repeat
Image.Pad Original size, no scaling

sourceSize: the most important performance setting#

A 4K wallpaper decoded at full size takes about 33 MB of memory. If you only show it as a 260×146 thumbnail, set sourceSize: Qt.size(520, 292) (2× for HiDPI) and it takes about 0.6 MB. Always set sourceSize for thumbnails, album art and avatars.

Status and loading#

Image {
    id: art
    source: player?.trackArtUrl ?? ""
    onStatusChanged: if (status === Image.Error) console.warn("failed to load", source)
}
Rectangle { visible: art.status !== Image.Ready; color: "#313244" }  // placeholder

status: Image.Null, Image.Loading, Image.Ready, Image.Error. progress is 0–1 while loading.

Reloading an image whose file changed#

Images are cached by URL. If a file at the same path changes (a symlinked wallpaper, a regenerated thumbnail), add a changing query string and disable the cache:

Image { cache: false; source: "file:///tmp/cover.png?" + version }   // bump `version` to reload

Image sources#

  • Files: file:///absolute/path.png
  • Relative to the QML file: "assets/logo.svg"
  • Icon theme: "image://icon/firefox" or Quickshell.iconPath()
  • HTTP(S): "https://…" (Qt downloads it; MPRIS art URLs are often like this)
  • Data URLs: "data:image/png;base64,…"

For icons, prefer Quickshell's IconImage, which keeps them square, crisp and correctly sized.

AnimatedImage#

For GIFs and animated WebP:

AnimatedImage { source: "file:///home/me/Pictures/cat.gif"; playing: visible; speed: 1.0 }

SVG images#

SVGs need qt6-svg. Set sourceSize to the display size (times the device pixel ratio) so they rasterize sharply:

Image { source: "icons/logo.svg"; sourceSize: Qt.size(width * 2, height * 2) }

Putting it together: a media card#

MediaCard.qmlimport QtQuick
import Quickshell.Widgets

Rectangle {
    id: root
    property string title: "Song title that is quite long"
    property string artist: "Artist name"
    property url art: ""

    implicitWidth: 320; implicitHeight: 84
    radius: 18
    gradient: Gradient {
        orientation: Gradient.Horizontal
        GradientStop { position: 0; color: "#313244" }
        GradientStop { position: 1; color: "#1e1e2e" }
    }
    border.color: "#45475a"

    ClippingRectangle {                       // rounded clip for the image
        id: cover
        x: 10; anchors.verticalCenter: parent.verticalCenter
        width: 64; height: 64; radius: 12
        color: "#45475a"
        Image {
            anchors.fill: parent
            source: root.art
            fillMode: Image.PreserveAspectCrop
            sourceSize: Qt.size(128, 128)
            asynchronous: true
        }
    }
    Column {
        anchors { left: cover.right; leftMargin: 12; right: parent.right; rightMargin: 12; verticalCenter: parent.verticalCenter }
        spacing: 2
        Text { width: parent.width; text: root.title; color: "#cdd6f4"; font.pixelSize: 15; font.weight: Font.DemiBold; elide: Text.ElideRight }
        Text { width: parent.width; text: root.artist; color: "#a6adc8"; font.pixelSize: 13; elide: Text.ElideRight }
    }
}
Exercises
  1. Make a pill-shaped badge with an outline only (color: "transparent").
  2. Make a Text that shows at most two lines of a long string and ends with "…".
  3. Show your wallpaper as a 300×170 rounded thumbnail with PreserveAspectCrop and a proper sourceSize.
Part III · Qt Quick: Drawing Things

Sizing and Implicit Size

"Why is my component zero pixels wide?" "Why won't my layout stretch?" "Binding loop detected for width?" These questions all come from one concept: the difference between implicit size and actual size.

Two sizes for every item#

Meaning Who sets it
implicitWidth, implicitHeight The size the item would like to be, based on its content The item itself (Text from its text, Image from its picture, your component from its children)
width, height The size it actually is Whoever places it: you, anchors, or a layout

By default, width follows implicitWidth. Set width explicitly (or let anchors or a layout set it) and the implicit size is just a hint.

Text { text: "Hello" }                 // implicitWidth ≈ 36, width = 36 (follows)
Text { text: "Hello"; width: 200 }     // implicitWidth ≈ 36, width = 200 (overridden)
Rectangle { }                          // implicit 0×0, so invisible!
Item { }                               // implicit 0×0

Which types have an implicit size?#

Type Implicit size comes from
Text the laid-out text
Image the picture (or sourceSize)
Row, Column, Grid, Flow their children plus spacing
RowLayout, ColumnLayout children's preferred sizes plus spacing
Controls (Button, Slider…) their content and style
Rectangle, Item, MouseArea nothing: 0×0 unless you set it
Your components whatever you set on the root's implicitWidth/implicitHeight

Rule 1: components size themselves with implicit size#

When you write a component, set implicitWidth/implicitHeight on its root, computed from its content. Don't set width/height on your own root.

Chip.qmlimport QtQuick

Rectangle {
    id: root
    property alias text: label.text

    implicitWidth: label.implicitWidth + 24     // content + padding
    implicitHeight: label.implicitHeight + 10
    radius: height / 2
    color: "#313244"

    Text { id: label; anchors.centerIn: parent; color: "white" }
}

Now a Chip is exactly as wide as its text plus padding, and users can still stretch it with width:, anchors or Layout.fillWidth. If you'd written width: label.implicitWidth + 24 instead, a layout couldn't override it (or you'd get warnings), and the chip couldn't be stretched.

Rule 2: users of a component set the actual size#

Chip { text: "auto size" }                          // uses implicit size
Chip { text: "fixed"; width: 120 }                  // forced width
RowLayout { Chip { text: "fills"; Layout.fillWidth: true } }   // layout decides

Rule 3: Quickshell windows use implicit size#

For PanelWindow, FloatingWindow and PopupWindow, set implicitWidth/implicitHeight. (The window's width/height exist too, but implicit size is the recommended way to request a size.) An anchored edge overrides the matching dimension: a bar anchored left and right gets the screen width automatically, so you only set implicitHeight.

PanelWindow {
    anchors { top: true; left: true; right: true }
    implicitHeight: 36                   // width comes from the anchors
}
PanelWindow {                            // unanchored popup: set both
    implicitWidth: 400
    implicitHeight: content.implicitHeight + 32   // grows with content
}

Sizing a window to its content#

A common pattern for popups and notifications:

PanelWindow {
    implicitWidth: 360
    implicitHeight: Math.max(1, column.implicitHeight + 24)   // never 0 (an invalid surface)
    Column { id: column; x: 12; y: 12; width: parent.width - 24; spacing: 8 /* … */ }
}

Binding loops and how to avoid them#

QML Item: Binding loop detected for property "implicitWidth"

This happens when a size depends on itself through a cycle, e.g. a parent's implicit width comes from a child whose width comes from the parent:

Rectangle {
    implicitWidth: inner.width + 20       // parent ← child
    Text { id: inner; width: parent.width - 20 }   // child ← parent ✗ loop
}

Fix: build implicit sizes from the content's implicit sizes, and make actual sizes flow from parent to child:

Rectangle {
    implicitWidth: inner.implicitWidth + 20        // from the text's natural size ✓
    Text { id: inner; anchors.centerIn: parent }   // positioned, not sized from parent
}

The mental model: implicit sizes flow up (children tell parents what they'd like), actual sizes flow down (parents tell children what they get). Never mix directions on the same axis.

childrenRect#

childrenRect is the bounding box of an item's children. It's a quick way to size a plain Item around absolutely positioned children: implicitWidth: childrenRect.width. Prefer positioners or layouts when you can, because childrenRect makes loops easy.

Pixel snapping and HiDPI#

  • Quickshell windows report devicePixelRatio (e.g. 1.5 at 150% scale). Qt scales automatically; you write sizes in logical pixels.
  • Odd sizes at fractional scaling can blur 1 px lines. Keep borders and dividers at whole logical pixels and consider border.pixelAligned: true.
  • For images and SVGs, set sourceSize to display size × devicePixelRatio for crispness.
Exercises
  1. Build Chip.qml and put three chips with different text lengths in a Row. They should all size themselves.
  2. Put one chip in a RowLayout with Layout.fillWidth: true and confirm it stretches.
  3. Create a binding loop on purpose, read the warning, then fix it using implicit sizes.
Part III · Qt Quick: Drawing Things

Anchors

Anchors glue an item's edges to other items' edges. They're the most common way to position things in QML, and they automatically follow when sizes change.

Anchor lines#

Every item has seven invisible anchor lines:

You attach your lines to another item's lines (your parent or a sibling):

Rectangle {
    id: bar
    width: 600; height: 40; color: "#1e1e2e"

    Text {
        id: title
        anchors.left: parent.left          // my left edge = parent's left edge
        anchors.leftMargin: 12             // …plus 12 px
        anchors.verticalCenter: parent.verticalCenter
        text: "left"; color: "white"
    }
    Text {
        anchors.centerIn: parent           // shortcut: both centers
        text: "center"; color: "white"
    }
    Text {
        anchors.right: parent.right
        anchors.rightMargin: 12
        anchors.verticalCenter: parent.verticalCenter
        text: "right"; color: "white"
    }
    Rectangle {                             // a divider right after the title
        anchors.left: title.right
        anchors.leftMargin: 8
        anchors.top: parent.top; anchors.bottom: parent.bottom
        anchors.margins: 10                 // applies to every anchored side
        width: 1; color: "#45475a"
    }
}

All anchor properties#

Property Meaning
anchors.left / right / top / bottom Attach an edge
anchors.horizontalCenter / verticalCenter Attach a center line
anchors.baseline Attach text baselines (align texts of different sizes)
anchors.fill: item All four edges = fill that item
anchors.centerIn: item Both centers = center inside that item
anchors.margins Margin for all anchored edges
anchors.leftMargin / rightMargin / topMargin / bottomMargin Per-edge margin
anchors.horizontalCenterOffset / verticalCenterOffset Shift a centered item
anchors.baselineOffset Shift the baseline
anchors.alignWhenCentered Snap centered items to whole pixels (default true)

Stretching with two anchors#

Anchor opposite edges and the item stretches between them, so you don't set that dimension:

Rectangle {
    anchors.left: parent.left
    anchors.right: parent.right          // width now comes from the anchors
    anchors.top: parent.top
    height: 40                           // only the height is set by hand
}
Text {
    anchors.left: icon.right; anchors.leftMargin: 8
    anchors.right: parent.right; anchors.rightMargin: 8   // a bounded width
    elide: Text.ElideRight                                // so elide works
}

Rules#

  1. You can anchor only to your parent or siblings (items with the same parent).
  2. Don't combine anchors with explicit x/y or width/height on the same axis. Anchors win and QML prints warnings.
  3. Don't anchor items managed by Row/Column/layouts on the axis the layout controls. Use Layout.* properties instead.
  4. Anchors are bindings: when the target moves or resizes, you follow.

Changing anchors at runtime#

Anchors can be bound to conditions:

Rectangle {
    property bool bottomBar: false
    anchors.top: bottomBar ? undefined : parent.top       // undefined = remove the anchor
    anchors.bottom: bottomBar ? parent.bottom : undefined
}

For animated anchor changes use AnchorChanges inside states plus an AnchorAnimation (Animation II: States, Transitions, Sequences).

The truly centered clock#

A classic bar problem: in a row of left, center and right modules, the center module isn't centered on screen when the left and right sides have different widths. Anchors solve it:

PanelWindow {
    anchors { top: true; left: true; right: true }
    implicitHeight: 36

    Row { anchors.left: parent.left;  anchors.leftMargin: 8;  anchors.verticalCenter: parent.verticalCenter; spacing: 8 /* workspaces… */ }
    Text { anchors.centerIn: parent; text: "12:34" }        // always the exact center of the bar
    Row { anchors.right: parent.right; anchors.rightMargin: 8; anchors.verticalCenter: parent.verticalCenter; spacing: 8 /* tray… */ }
}

Quickshell window "anchors" are different#

PanelWindow has its own anchors group with boolean members (top, bottom, left, right) that attach the window to screen edges. Same word, different thing:

PanelWindow {
    anchors.top: true            // window: glue to the top screen edge (a bool)
    Text {
        anchors.top: parent.top  // item: glue to the parent's top line (an anchor line)
    }
}
Exercises
  1. Build a bar with left, center and right groups using only anchors.
  2. Make a notification-like card: icon on the left, title and body to its right that elide at the card's right edge.
  3. Add a property bool vertical that switches a small indicator between the top-right and bottom-left corners of a rectangle, using conditional anchors.
Part III · Qt Quick: Drawing Things

Positioners and Layouts

Anchors are great for a few items. For rows of modules, grids of toggles and lists of buttons, use positioners (simple stacking) or layouts (stacking plus stretching).

Positioners: Row, Column, Grid, Flow#

Positioners place children one after another using each child's own size. They're simple and cheap.

Row {
    spacing: 8                       // gap between children
    padding: 4                       // space around all children
    Rectangle { width: 30; height: 30; color: "#f38ba8" }
    Rectangle { width: 50; height: 30; color: "#a6e3a1" }
    Rectangle { width: 20; height: 30; color: "#89b4fa" }
}

Column { spacing: 4 /* stacked top to bottom */ }

Grid {
    columns: 3                       // or rows: 2
    spacing: 6
    // fills row by row: items 1 2 3 / 4 5 6
}

Flow {
    width: 200                       // wraps like text when a row is full
    spacing: 4
}
Positioner property Meaning
spacing Gap between items
padding, leftPadding… Inner padding
layoutDirection Qt.LeftToRight or Qt.RightToLeft (Row, Grid, Flow)
columns, rows, flow Grid shape and fill order
horizontalItemAlignment, verticalItemAlignment Grid alignment
add, move, populate Transitions when children appear or move (Animation II: States, Transitions, Sequences)

Rules:

  • Children must have a size (implicit or explicit).
  • Don't set x (in a Row) or y (in a Column) on children: the positioner controls them.
  • To vertically center children of a Row, give each child anchors.verticalCenter: parent.verticalCenter.
  • Invisible children (visible: false) take no space, which is perfect for optional modules.

Layouts: RowLayout, ColumnLayout, GridLayout#

import QtQuick.Layouts. Layouts do what positioners do plus stretching, alignment and min/max sizes, controlled by attached Layout.* properties on each child.

import QtQuick
import QtQuick.Layouts

RowLayout {
    anchors.fill: parent
    anchors.margins: 6
    spacing: 8

    Rectangle { Layout.preferredWidth: 32; Layout.fillHeight: true; color: "#cba6f7" }   // fixed width
    Rectangle { Layout.fillWidth: true;    Layout.fillHeight: true; color: "#313244" }   // takes the rest
    Rectangle { Layout.preferredWidth: 80; Layout.preferredHeight: 20; color: "#a6e3a1"
                Layout.alignment: Qt.AlignVCenter }                                     // centered vertically
}

All Layout attached properties#

Property Meaning
Layout.fillWidth / fillHeight Grow to take available space
Layout.preferredWidth / preferredHeight Desired size (default: implicit size)
Layout.minimumWidth / minimumHeight Never smaller than this
Layout.maximumWidth / maximumHeight Never larger than this (great with elided text)
Layout.alignment Qt.AlignLeft, AlignRight, AlignHCenter, AlignTop, AlignBottom, AlignVCenter, combine with |
Layout.margins, leftMargin, rightMargin, topMargin, bottomMargin Extra space around this item
Layout.horizontalStretchFactor / verticalStretchFactor Share extra space unequally between fillers (Qt 6.5+)
Layout.row, column, rowSpan, columnSpan Placement in a GridLayout
Layout.uniformCellWidths / uniformCellHeights On the layout itself: equal cells

Spacers#

An empty Item that fills pushes things apart:

RowLayout {
    Text { text: "left" }
    Item { Layout.fillWidth: true }      // spacer
    Text { text: "right" }
}

GridLayout: a quick-settings grid#

GridLayout {
    columns: 2
    rowSpacing: 8; columnSpacing: 8
    Repeater {
        model: ["Wi-Fi", "Bluetooth", "Do not disturb", "Night light", "Caffeine", "Airplane"]
        Rectangle {
            required property string modelData
            Layout.fillWidth: true
            Layout.preferredHeight: 52
            radius: 16; color: "#313244"
            Text { anchors.centerIn: parent; text: parent.modelData; color: "white" }
        }
    }
}

StackLayout: one child at a time#

StackLayout {
    currentIndex: tabs.currentIndex          // show page 0, 1 or 2
    Rectangle { color: "#f38ba8" }
    Rectangle { color: "#a6e3a1" }
    Rectangle { color: "#89b4fa" }
}

Positioners or layouts?#

Need Use
Items stacked at their natural size Row / Column
Something must stretch, or needs min/max sizes RowLayout / ColumnLayout
Wrapping tags or chips Flow
Grid of equal tiles GridLayout with fillWidth, or Grid with fixed sizes
Tabs or pages StackLayout (or a Loader to save memory)
Precise overlapping placement anchors

A full bar layout#

~/.config/quickshell/playground/shell.qmlimport Quickshell
import QtQuick
import QtQuick.Layouts

PanelWindow {
    anchors { top: true; left: true; right: true }
    implicitHeight: 38
    color: "#11111b"

    component Chip: Rectangle {
        property alias text: t.text
        implicitWidth: t.implicitWidth + 20; implicitHeight: 26
        radius: 13; color: "#313244"
        Text { id: t; anchors.centerIn: parent; color: "#cdd6f4"; font.pixelSize: 12 }
    }

    RowLayout {                                   // left group
        anchors { left: parent.left; leftMargin: 8; verticalCenter: parent.verticalCenter }
        spacing: 6
        Chip { text: "1" } Chip { text: "2" } Chip { text: "3" }
        Text {
            text: "kitty — ~/projects/quickshell/very/long/path/that/goes/on"
            color: "#a6adc8"; elide: Text.ElideRight
            Layout.maximumWidth: 260                // cap the width so elide kicks in
        }
    }

    Chip { anchors.centerIn: parent; text: "Fri 21 Nov  14:32" }   // true center

    RowLayout {                                   // right group
        anchors { right: parent.right; rightMargin: 8; verticalCenter: parent.verticalCenter }
        spacing: 6
        Chip { text: "wifi" } Chip { text: "vol 62%" } Chip { text: "bat 81%" }
    }
}
Exercises
  1. Make a ColumnLayout sidebar: a header with fixed height, a list area that fills, and a footer with fixed height.
  2. Build a 3×2 GridLayout of toggle tiles that stretch to the window width.
  3. Hide one chip in the right group with visible: false and watch the others close the gap.
Part III · Qt Quick: Drawing Things

Models, Repeater and ListView

Workspaces, tray icons, notifications, apps, Wi-Fi networks, media players: shells are full of lists of things. QML handles them with models (the data), delegates (a template per item) and views (Repeater, ListView, GridView) that combine the two.

Repeater#

Repeater creates one delegate per model entry, places them in its parent, and keeps them in sync with the model.

Model = a number#

Row {
    spacing: 6
    Repeater {
        model: 5                                  // 5 copies, index 0..4
        Rectangle {
            required property int index           // provided by the Repeater
            width: 24; height: 24; radius: 12
            color: index === 2 ? "#cba6f7" : "#45475a"
            Text { anchors.centerIn: parent; text: parent.index + 1; color: "white" }
        }
    }
}

Model = a JS array#

Column {
    Repeater {
        model: ["Firefox", "Kitty", "Spotify"]
        Text {
            required property string modelData    // the array element
            required property int index
            text: (index + 1) + ". " + modelData
            color: "white"
        }
    }
}

Model = an array of objects#

Repeater {
    model: [
        { icon: "wifi",       label: "Wi-Fi",     on: true },
        { icon: "bluetooth",  label: "Bluetooth", on: false }
    ]
    Row {
        required property var modelData
        spacing: 6
        Text { text: modelData.icon; font.family: "Material Symbols Rounded"; color: modelData.on ? "#a6e3a1" : "#6c7086" }
        Text { text: modelData.label; color: "white" }
    }
}

Model = a Quickshell ObjectModel#

Quickshell's lists (workspaces, tray items, players, devices, notifications) are ObjectModels. Pass them directly:

import Quickshell.Services.SystemTray
import Quickshell.Widgets

Row {
    Repeater {
        model: SystemTray.items
        IconImage {
            required property SystemTrayItem modelData    // each element is a SystemTrayItem
            implicitSize: 18
            source: modelData.icon
        }
    }
}

required properties in delegates#

A delegate receives its data through these names:

Name Available when Meaning
index always position in the model
modelData arrays, ObjectModels, numbers the element itself
role names ListModel / C++ models each field directly (e.g. title)

Always declare them with required property. That makes the data explicit, gives you types and autocomplete, and is required for some models in Qt 6.

Repeater properties#

Property / method Meaning
model The data
delegate The template (implicit when you write a child)
count Number of created items
itemAt(i) The delegate object at index i
onItemAdded(index, item) / onItemRemoved Signals

ListModel: a mutable list you control#

When you own the list (history, todo items, a custom menu) and want to add or remove entries with nice animations:

ListModel {
    id: todos
    ListElement { title: "Rice the bar"; done: true }
    ListElement { title: "Lock screen"; done: false }
}

// later, in JS:
todos.append({ title: "Launcher", done: false })
todos.insert(0, { title: "First!", done: false })
todos.remove(1)
todos.setProperty(0, "done", true)
todos.move(0, 2, 1)
todos.clear()
todos.count        // number of entries
todos.get(0).title // read an entry

Delegates receive role names directly: required property string title, required property bool done.

ListView: scrolling lists#

Repeater creates everything at once. ListView creates only the delegates that are visible, scrolls, and supports keyboard navigation, highlights and transitions. Use it for anything that might be long (apps, notifications, clipboard history).

ListView {
    id: list
    width: 300; height: 400
    clip: true                                 // don't draw outside the view
    spacing: 4
    model: DesktopEntries.applications         // ObjectModel of DesktopEntry
    delegate: Rectangle {
        required property DesktopEntry modelData
        required property int index
        width: ListView.view.width             // attached: the view this delegate is in
        height: 40; radius: 8
        color: ListView.isCurrentItem ? "#45475a" : "transparent"
        Text { anchors.verticalCenter: parent.verticalCenter; x: 12; text: modelData.name; color: "white" }
        MouseArea { anchors.fill: parent; onClicked: list.currentIndex = index }
    }
}

Important ListView properties#

Property Meaning
model, delegate Data and template
orientation ListView.Vertical (default) or ListView.Horizontal
spacing Gap between delegates
currentIndex, currentItem Selection
highlight, highlightFollowsCurrentItem, highlightMoveDuration A moving selection rectangle
keyNavigationEnabled, keyNavigationWraps Arrow keys move the selection
clip Cut delegates at the view's edges (almost always true)
interactive Allow drag/flick scrolling
boundsBehavior Flickable.StopAtBounds stops the "rubber band" overscroll
cacheBuffer Pixels of off-screen delegates to keep alive
header, footer, section.* Extra items and grouping
verticalLayoutDirection ListView.BottomToTop for chat-like lists
add, remove, displaced, move Transitions for model changes
contentY, contentHeight, atYEnd Scroll state

Methods: positionViewAtIndex(i, ListView.Contain), positionViewAtEnd(), incrementCurrentIndex(), decrementCurrentIndex(), indexAt(x, y), itemAtIndex(i).

Attached in delegates: ListView.view, ListView.isCurrentItem, ListView.onAdd, ListView.onRemove.

A keyboard-driven list with highlight#

ListView {
    id: list
    focus: true
    keyNavigationEnabled: true
    highlight: Rectangle { radius: 10; color: "#45475a" }
    highlightMoveDuration: 120
    Keys.onReturnPressed: console.log("chose", model[currentIndex])
    model: ["one", "two", "three"]
    delegate: Text { required property string modelData; text: modelData; color: "white"; padding: 10 }
}

Animating additions and removals#

ListView {
    add: Transition { NumberAnimation { properties: "opacity"; from: 0; to: 1; duration: 200 }
                      NumberAnimation { properties: "x"; from: 100; duration: 250; easing.type: Easing.OutCubic } }
    remove: Transition { NumberAnimation { properties: "opacity"; to: 0; duration: 150 } }
    displaced: Transition { NumberAnimation { properties: "y"; duration: 200; easing.type: Easing.OutCubic } }
}

These transitions only work when the model reports which items changed (ListModel, Quickshell ObjectModel, ScriptModel). A plain JS array that you reassign replaces everything at once; ObjectModel and ScriptModel shows how ScriptModel fixes that.

GridView#

Like ListView, but in a grid. Good for wallpaper pickers and app grids:

GridView {
    width: 600; height: 400; clip: true
    cellWidth: 150; cellHeight: 100
    model: wallpapers
    delegate: Image {
        required property string modelData
        width: 140; height: 90
        source: "file://" + modelData
        fillMode: Image.PreserveAspectCrop
        sourceSize: Qt.size(280, 180)
        asynchronous: true
    }
}

Flickable and ScrollView#

To scroll arbitrary content (not a list), wrap it in a Flickable:

Flickable {
    width: 300; height: 400; clip: true
    contentWidth: column.width; contentHeight: column.height
    boundsBehavior: Flickable.StopAtBounds
    Column { id: column; width: 300 /* lots of content */ }
}

ScrollView (from Controls) is a Flickable with styled scrollbars.

Never store state in delegates#

Delegates are created and destroyed as you scroll or as the model changes. A property bool expanded inside a delegate is lost when it scrolls away. Store per-item state in the model, or in a JS object keyed by id in a parent or singleton.

Exercises
  1. Show workspaces 1–10 with a Repeater and model: 10, highlighting number 3.
  2. Build a ListModel todo list with a button that appends entries, and animate additions.
  3. Show all installed apps in a ListView (DesktopEntries.applications) with arrow-key navigation and a highlight.
Part III · Qt Quick: Drawing Things

Mouse, Touchpad and Keyboard Input

A rice that only shows things is a wallpaper. This chapter covers clicks, hover, scrolling, dragging and keyboard input, and the Quickshell-specific rule about keyboard focus.

MouseArea: the classic#

MouseArea is an invisible item that receives mouse events inside its bounds. Usually you fill a parent with it:

Rectangle {
    id: btn
    width: 120; height: 36; radius: 10
    color: area.pressed ? "#585b70" : area.containsMouse ? "#45475a" : "#313244"

    MouseArea {
        id: area
        anchors.fill: parent
        hoverEnabled: true                     // REQUIRED for containsMouse / onEntered without pressing
        cursorShape: Qt.PointingHandCursor     // hand cursor on hover
        acceptedButtons: Qt.LeftButton | Qt.RightButton | Qt.MiddleButton

        onClicked: mouse => {
            if (mouse.button === Qt.LeftButton) console.log("left")
            else if (mouse.button === Qt.RightButton) console.log("right")
            else console.log("middle")
        }
        onDoubleClicked: console.log("double")
        onPressAndHold: console.log("long press")       // after pressAndHoldInterval ms
        onEntered: console.log("mouse in")
        onExited: console.log("mouse out")
        onWheel: wheel => console.log("scroll", wheel.angleDelta.y)
    }
}

MouseArea properties#

Property Meaning
hoverEnabled Track hover without a button pressed
containsMouse Pointer is inside (needs hoverEnabled unless pressed)
pressed, pressedButtons Currently held
acceptedButtons Which buttons to react to
cursorShape Qt.PointingHandCursor, Qt.IBeamCursor, Qt.SizeHorCursor…
mouseX, mouseY Pointer position inside the area
drag.target, drag.axis, drag.minimumX… Built-in dragging
propagateComposedEvents Let clicks pass to areas underneath
preventStealing Keep the grab during drags
pressAndHoldInterval Long-press time in ms
scrollGestureEnabled Accept touchpad scroll gestures

The event objects#

  • MouseEvent (clicked, pressed…): button, buttons, modifiers, x, y, wasHeld, accepted
  • WheelEvent (wheel): angleDelta.x/.y (mouse wheel, 120 per notch), pixelDelta (touchpads), modifiers, inverted

Scrolling to change a value (mouse and touchpad)#

A wheel notch is angleDelta.y = ±120, while touchpads send many small values. Normalize:

MouseArea {
    anchors.fill: parent
    property real acc: 0
    onWheel: w => {
        acc += w.angleDelta.y
        while (Math.abs(acc) >= 120) {                 // one "step" per notch-equivalent
            Audio.setVolume(Audio.volume + (acc > 0 ? 0.05 : -0.05))
            acc -= 120 * Math.sign(acc)
        }
    }
}

Pointer handlers: the modern way#

Handlers are lighter than MouseArea and combine: several handlers on one item don't block each other.

Rectangle {
    width: 100; height: 40; radius: 8
    color: hover.hovered ? "#45475a" : "#313244"

    HoverHandler { id: hover; cursorShape: Qt.PointingHandCursor }
    TapHandler { onTapped: console.log("left tap") }
    TapHandler { acceptedButtons: Qt.RightButton; onTapped: console.log("right tap") }
    TapHandler { onDoubleTapped: console.log("double"); onLongPressed: console.log("hold") }
    WheelHandler { onWheel: e => console.log(e.angleDelta.y) }
    DragHandler { target: parent }                    // drag the rectangle around
}
Handler Key properties / signals
HoverHandler hovered, point.position, cursorShape, acceptedDevices
TapHandler onTapped(eventPoint, button), onDoubleTapped, onLongPressed, pressed, acceptedButtons, gesturePolicy
WheelHandler onWheel(event), property/target to auto-adjust a property, rotationScale
DragHandler target, xAxis.minimum/maximum, active, translation
PinchHandler touchpad/touch pinch zoom and rotate
PointHandler low-level pointer tracking
Which to use?

Use HoverHandler for hover effects (it never steals clicks), TapHandler for clicks, WheelHandler for scroll. Fall back to MouseArea when you need containsMouse and pressed together, propagation control, or the built-in drag.

Drag and drop#

Rectangle {
    id: card
    width: 80; height: 50; color: "#cba6f7"
    Drag.active: dragArea.drag.active
    Drag.hotSpot: Qt.point(width / 2, height / 2)
    Drag.keys: ["window"]
    property string payload: "0x55d1a2"
    MouseArea { id: dragArea; anchors.fill: parent; drag.target: parent
                onReleased: parent.Drag.drop() }
}

DropArea {
    width: 200; height: 120
    keys: ["window"]
    Rectangle { anchors.fill: parent; color: parent.containsDrag ? "#45475a" : "#313244" }
    onDropped: drop => console.log("dropped", drop.source.payload)
}

You'll use this to move windows between workspaces in the overview (Project: Workspace Overview).

Keyboard input#

Keys go to the item with active focus:

Item {
    focus: true                                     // ask for focus within this window
    Keys.onPressed: event => {
        if (event.key === Qt.Key_Escape) close()
        else if (event.key === Qt.Key_K && (event.modifiers & Qt.ControlModifier)) up()
        else return
        event.accepted = true                       // stop propagation
    }
    Keys.onReturnPressed: launch()
    Keys.onUpPressed: list.decrementCurrentIndex()
    Keys.onDownPressed: list.incrementCurrentIndex()
    Keys.onTabPressed: next()
}

Common keys: Qt.Key_Escape, Key_Return, Key_Enter, Key_Tab, Key_Backtab, Key_Up/Down/Left/Right, Key_Backspace, Key_Delete, Key_Home, Key_End, Key_PageUp/PageDown, Key_Space, Key_A…Key_Z, Key_0…Key_9, Key_F1… Modifiers: Qt.ShiftModifier, ControlModifier, AltModifier, MetaModifier (Super).

event.text gives the typed character, useful for "press the first letter" shortcuts.

Focus#

  • focus: true requests focus within its focus scope; activeFocus is true when it actually has it.
  • forceActiveFocus() grabs focus immediately (call it when a popup opens).
  • FocusScope groups items so a component can manage focus internally.
  • KeyNavigation.tab: otherItem / KeyNavigation.down define arrow and tab order.

Text input#

import QtQuick
import QtQuick.Controls

TextField {                           // styled, from Controls
    placeholderText: "Search…"
    onTextChanged: search(text)
    onAccepted: launch()              // Enter pressed
}

TextInput {                           // bare, unstyled (style it yourself)
    width: 300
    color: "white"
    font.pixelSize: 16
    focus: true
    echoMode: TextInput.Password      // Normal, Password, NoEcho, PasswordEchoOnEdit
    passwordCharacter: "●"
    selectByMouse: true
    validator: IntValidator { bottom: 0; top: 100 }   // only numbers 0–100
    Keys.onEscapePressed: text = ""
}

For multi-line input use TextArea (Controls) or TextEdit.

Quickshell rule: windows need keyboard focus#

This catches everyone once. A layer-shell window doesn't receive keyboard input unless it asks for it. Even with focus: true on a TextInput, typing goes to the app behind it until you set:

import Quickshell.Wayland

PanelWindow {
    WlrLayershell.keyboardFocus: WlrKeyboardFocus.Exclusive   // grab all keys while open (launchers, lock-like UIs)
    // or WlrKeyboardFocus.OnDemand: focus when clicked (search box in a sidebar)
    // default WlrKeyboardFocus.None: never takes keys (bars)
    TextInput { focus: true }
}

PanelWindow also has a simpler focusable property, and WlrLayershell documents the exact behavior of each mode.

Don't leave Exclusive on

A window with Exclusive keyboard focus blocks typing into every other app. Only use it while the window is visible and open (launchers, power menus), and make sure Esc closes it.

Closing popups by clicking outside#

Clicks outside your window go to other apps, so your window never sees them. Options:

  • On Hyprland: HyprlandFocusGrab tells you when the user clicks outside a set of windows.
  • Anywhere: a fullscreen transparent PanelWindow behind the popup that closes it on click.
Exercises
  1. Make a button with hover, press and right-click behavior using handlers only.
  2. Make a slider-like bar you can scroll to change a value, normalized for touchpads.
  3. Make a fullscreen overlay window with Exclusive keyboard focus that shows the name of every key you press and closes on Esc.
Part III · Qt Quick: Drawing Things

Qt Quick Controls and Restyling Them

import QtQuick.Controls gives you ready-made widgets: sliders, switches, buttons, text fields, scroll bars, combo boxes, tooltips. Out of the box they look generic, and rices restyle them completely. This chapter shows how.

Choosing a style#

Controls have several built-in styles (Basic, Fusion, Material, Universal, Imagine). For heavy restyling, use Basic: it's the simplest to override and doesn't fight you.

shell.qml//@ pragma Env QT_QUICK_CONTROLS_STYLE=Basic
import Quickshell

The pragma sets the environment variable before Quickshell starts (Shell Structure, Pragmas and Reloading).

The anatomy of a control#

Every control is made of replaceable parts:

Part What it is
background Item drawn behind everything (the track, the box)
contentItem The main visual (text of a button, track fill…)
handle / indicator The knob of a slider, the dot of a switch, the box of a checkbox
padding, leftPadding… Space between background and content
implicitWidth/Height Natural size

Override any part by assigning your own item.

Slider#

import QtQuick
import QtQuick.Controls

Slider {
    id: s
    from: 0; to: 1; value: 0.4
    stepSize: 0.01
    live: true                          // update `value` while dragging
    implicitWidth: 220; implicitHeight: 24

    onMoved: console.log("user moved to", value)    // only user interaction
    // onValueChanged fires on ANY change, including bindings

    background: Rectangle {
        x: s.leftPadding
        y: s.topPadding + s.availableHeight / 2 - height / 2
        width: s.availableWidth; height: 6; radius: 3
        color: "#45475a"
        Rectangle {                                         // filled part
            width: s.visualPosition * parent.width
            height: parent.height; radius: 3
            color: "#cba6f7"
        }
    }
    handle: Rectangle {
        x: s.leftPadding + s.visualPosition * (s.availableWidth - width)
        y: s.topPadding + s.availableHeight / 2 - height / 2
        width: 18; height: 18; radius: 9
        color: s.pressed ? "#f5e0dc" : "#cdd6f4"
        scale: s.pressed ? 1.15 : 1
        Behavior on scale { NumberAnimation { duration: 100 } }
    }
}

Useful Slider members: value, from, to, stepSize, visualPosition (0–1), position, pressed, orientation, snapMode, live, moved(), increase(), decrease().

Binding a slider to system state

value: Audio.volume plus onMoved: Audio.setVolume(value). Dragging calls your setter; external changes update the slider through the binding. Because the user-driven change only happens in onMoved, the binding on value survives.

A thick M3-style slider#

Slider {
    id: big
    from: 0; to: 1; value: 0.6
    implicitHeight: 40
    background: Rectangle {
        anchors.fill: parent; radius: 20; color: "#313244"
        Rectangle { width: Math.max(height, big.visualPosition * parent.width); height: parent.height
                    radius: 20; color: "#cba6f7" }
    }
    handle: Item {}                                  // no knob at all
}

Switch#

Switch {
    id: sw
    checked: Bluetooth.defaultAdapter?.enabled ?? false
    onToggled: Bluetooth.defaultAdapter.enabled = checked
    indicator: Rectangle {
        implicitWidth: 46; implicitHeight: 26
        x: sw.leftPadding; y: parent.height / 2 - height / 2
        radius: 13
        color: sw.checked ? "#cba6f7" : "#45475a"
        Behavior on color { ColorAnimation { duration: 150 } }
        Rectangle {
            x: sw.checked ? parent.width - width - 3 : 3
            anchors.verticalCenter: parent.verticalCenter
            width: 20; height: 20; radius: 10
            color: sw.checked ? "#1e1e2e" : "#cdd6f4"
            Behavior on x { NumberAnimation { duration: 150; easing.type: Easing.OutCubic } }
        }
    }
    contentItem: Item {}                            // no label
}

checked, toggled() (user), checkedChanged (any), toggle().

Button#

Button {
    id: b
    text: "Apply"
    onClicked: apply()
    background: Rectangle {
        implicitWidth: 100; implicitHeight: 36; radius: 18
        color: b.down ? "#b4befe" : b.hovered ? "#cba6f7" : "#89b4fa"
    }
    contentItem: Text { text: b.text; color: "#1e1e2e"; font.bold: true
                        horizontalAlignment: Text.AlignHCenter; verticalAlignment: Text.AlignVCenter }
}

down, hovered, pressed, checkable, checked, icon.name, icon.source, flat, clicked(), pressAndHold(), doubleClicked().

In shells most "buttons" are just a Rectangle + MouseArea or handlers, which is lighter and fully custom. Use Button when you want built-in keyboard activation and accessibility.

TextField#

TextField {
    id: tf
    placeholderText: "Search apps…"
    placeholderTextColor: "#6c7086"
    color: "#cdd6f4"
    font.pixelSize: 15
    leftPadding: 40
    background: Rectangle { implicitHeight: 44; radius: 22; color: "#313244"
                            border.width: tf.activeFocus ? 2 : 0; border.color: "#cba6f7" }
    Text { x: 14; anchors.verticalCenter: parent.verticalCenter; text: "search"
           font.family: "Material Symbols Rounded"; color: "#a6adc8" }
    onAccepted: console.log("enter:", text)
}

Other controls you'll use#

Control Use in shells Key members
CheckBox settings lists checked, checkState, tristate
RadioButton + ButtonGroup pick one of N checked, ButtonGroup.group
ComboBox dropdown (audio device picker) model, currentIndex, currentText, textRole, activated(index)
SpinBox numeric settings value, from, to, stepSize
ProgressBar download / progress value, from, to, indeterminate
BusyIndicator loading spinner running
ScrollView scrollable content contentWidth, ScrollBar.vertical.policy
ScrollBar attach to Flickable/ListView ScrollBar.vertical: ScrollBar { }
ToolTip hover hints ToolTip.visible, ToolTip.text, ToolTip.delay
TabBar + TabButton sidebar tabs currentIndex
StackView navigation stack (settings pages) push(), pop(), initialItem
SwipeView + PageIndicator swipeable pages currentIndex
Popup / Menu in-window popups open(), close(), modal
Dial, RangeSlider creative widgets value, first.value/second.value
Controls' Popup/Menu vs Quickshell PopupWindow

A Controls Popup or Menu lives inside its window and is clipped by the window's edges. In a 36 px bar, a Controls menu would be cut off! For anything that extends beyond the bar, use Quickshell's PopupWindow or QsMenuAnchor, which create a real separate surface (Popups, Anchors and Menus).

Make your own styled controls once#

Write StyledSlider.qml, StyledSwitch.qml, StyledTextField.qml in widgets/, reading colors from your theme singleton, then use them everywhere. That's exactly what end-4 (modules/common/widgets/) and Caelestia (components/) do. Building a Design System builds this library.

Exercises
  1. Build a restyled Slider and bind it to a property real level. Show Math.round(level*100)% next to it.
  2. Build a restyled Switch with an animated knob.
  3. Build a ComboBox listing ["Speakers", "Headphones", "HDMI"] and print the chosen one.
Part III · Qt Quick: Drawing Things

Animation I: Behaviors and Easing

Motion is what separates a "config" from a rice that feels alive: the workspace pill that slides, the panel that eases in, the icon that bounces on hover. Qt's animation system runs on the GPU and is easy to use.

Behavior: animate every change#

A Behavior says "whenever this property changes, animate to the new value instead of jumping":

Rectangle {
    width: expanded ? 240 : 40
    color: expanded ? "#cba6f7" : "#45475a"
    property bool expanded: hover.hovered
    HoverHandler { id: hover }

    Behavior on width { NumberAnimation { duration: 250; easing.type: Easing.OutCubic } }
    Behavior on color { ColorAnimation { duration: 200 } }
}

No matter why width changes (hover, a binding, a click), it animates. This is the single most useful animation tool in shells, and you can retrofit motion onto an existing bar by adding Behaviors.

// typical uses
Behavior on x       { NumberAnimation { duration: 300; easing.type: Easing.OutCubic } }   // sliding indicator
Behavior on opacity { NumberAnimation { duration: 150 } }                                 // fade
Behavior on scale   { NumberAnimation { duration: 120; easing.type: Easing.OutBack } }    // bounce
Behavior on radius  { NumberAnimation { duration: 250 } }                                 // shape morph
Behavior on implicitHeight { NumberAnimation { duration: 300; easing.type: Easing.OutCubic } } // grow with content

Disable a Behavior temporarily with enabled, e.g. to avoid animating on startup:

Behavior on x { enabled: root.ready; NumberAnimation { duration: 250 } }

Animation types#

Type Animates Notes
NumberAnimation numbers: x, y, width, opacity, scale, rotation… the workhorse
ColorAnimation colors interpolates in RGB
RotationAnimation rotation direction: RotationAnimation.Shortest avoids spinning the long way
PropertyAnimation anything (generic)
SmoothedAnimation follows a moving target smoothly velocity instead of duration
SpringAnimation physics spring spring, damping, mass, epsilon
Vector3dAnimation 3D vectors rare

Duration and easing#

duration is in milliseconds. Good defaults: 150 ms for hover and color, 250 ms for size and position, 350–500 ms for panels sliding in.

Easing shapes the speed over time. Linear motion looks robotic; real objects accelerate and decelerate.

Easing Feel Use for
Easing.OutCubic fast start, gentle stop the default for UI: panels, indicators
Easing.OutQuint / OutExpo very fast start, long glide snappy, modern
Easing.InOutQuad / InOutCubic smooth both ends looping, back-and-forth
Easing.OutBack overshoots, then settles playful bounces, scale-on-hover
Easing.InCubic slow start, fast end things leaving the screen
Easing.OutElastic springy wobble use sparingly
Easing.OutBounce bounces like a ball use sparingly
Easing.Linear constant speed spinners, progress
Easing.BezierSpline your own curve design-system curves (below) 
NumberAnimation {
    duration: 400
    easing.type: Easing.OutBack
    easing.overshoot: 1.6          // how far OutBack overshoots (default 1.70158)
}

Custom curves (Material 3 motion)#

Material Design 3 defines named curves as cubic Béziers. Use them with BezierSpline, writing the control points followed by the end point 1, 1:

NumberAnimation {
    duration: 450
    easing.type: Easing.BezierSpline
    easing.bezierCurve: [0.05, 0.7, 0.1, 1, 1, 1]     // M3 "emphasized decelerate"
}
M3 curve bezierCurve
Standard [0.2, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1]
Standard decelerate [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1]
Standard accelerate [0.3, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]
Emphasized decelerate [0.05, 0.7, 0.1, 1, 1, 1]
Emphasized accelerate [0.3, 0, 0.8, 0.15, 1, 1]
Expressive spatial (overshoot) [0.38, 1.21, 0.22, 1, 1, 1]
In the wild

end-4's Appearance.qml and Caelestia's appearance config define animation tokens like these (durations plus Bézier curves) once, and every component references them. You'll build the same in Motion Design.

Quickshell also has an EasingCurve helper type for evaluating curves in your own code.

Standalone animations#

Animations can also run on their own, not just as Behaviors.

"on property" syntax: start immediately or when told#

Rectangle {
    width: 20; height: 20; radius: 10; color: "#f38ba8"
    SequentialAnimation on opacity {          // animates THIS item's opacity
        running: recording                    // bind to state
        loops: Animation.Infinite
        NumberAnimation { to: 0.2; duration: 700; easing.type: Easing.InOutSine }
        NumberAnimation { to: 1.0; duration: 700; easing.type: Easing.InOutSine }
    }
}

Animation with an id: start from code#

Text {
    id: icon
    text: "notifications"
    font.family: "Material Symbols Rounded"

    SequentialAnimation {
        id: ring
        RotationAnimation { target: icon; to: 20; duration: 80 }
        RotationAnimation { target: icon; to: -20; duration: 120 }
        RotationAnimation { target: icon; to: 0; duration: 80 }
    }
}
// somewhere: ring.restart()  (e.g. when a notification arrives)

Animation control#

Member Meaning
running Bind or set to start and stop
loops Count, or Animation.Infinite
paused Pause or resume
alwaysRunToEnd Finish the cycle even when stopped
start(), stop(), restart(), pause(), resume(), complete() Methods
onStarted, onFinished, onStopped Signals
target / targets, property / properties, from, to What to animate

Hover effects cookbook#

// 1. grow on hover
scale: hover.hovered ? 1.08 : 1
Behavior on scale { NumberAnimation { duration: 150; easing.type: Easing.OutBack } }

// 2. background fades in
color: hover.hovered ? "#45475a" : "transparent"
Behavior on color { ColorAnimation { duration: 120 } }

// 3. pill expands to reveal a label
width: hover.hovered ? icon.width + label.implicitWidth + 24 : icon.width + 16
clip: true
Behavior on width { NumberAnimation { duration: 220; easing.type: Easing.OutCubic } }

// 4. icon fills in (Material Symbols variable FILL axis, Qt 6.7+)
font.variableAxes: ({ "FILL": hover.hovered ? 1 : 0 })

// 5. press feedback
scale: area.pressed ? 0.92 : 1

Performance#

  • Animate opacity, scale, x, y, rotation: they're nearly free on the GPU.
  • Animating width/height re-lays out children every frame. It's fine for small items, but be careful with big layouts.
  • Infinite animations keep the shell redrawing at 60+ fps. Bind running to visibility so they stop when hidden.
Exercises
  1. Make a workspace indicator: 5 dots, where the active one is a wide pill. Clicking a dot activates it, and the width changes animate with OutCubic.
  2. Make a "recording" dot that pulses only while property bool recording is true.
  3. Make a notification bell icon that wiggles (SequentialAnimation of rotations) when you click it.
Part III · Qt Quick: Drawing Things

Animation II: States, Transitions, Sequences

Behaviors animate single properties. For coordinated motion (a panel that slides in while fading and then reveals its content), use states, transitions and grouped animations.

Grouped animations#

SequentialAnimation {           // one after another
    NumberAnimation { target: panel; property: "x"; to: 0; duration: 300; easing.type: Easing.OutCubic }
    PauseAnimation { duration: 100 }
    NumberAnimation { target: content; property: "opacity"; to: 1; duration: 200 }
}

ParallelAnimation {             // at the same time
    NumberAnimation { target: panel; property: "y"; to: 0; duration: 350 }
    NumberAnimation { target: panel; property: "opacity"; to: 1; duration: 250 }
}

Nest them freely. Helper steps inside sequences:

Step Does
PauseAnimation { duration } wait
ScriptAction { script: doSomething() } run code at that moment
PropertyAction { target; property; value } set a property instantly (e.g. visible: true before fading in)

Fade out, then hide#

SequentialAnimation {
    id: hideAnim
    NumberAnimation { target: osd; property: "opacity"; to: 0; duration: 200 }
    PropertyAction { target: osd; property: "visible"; value: false }
}

States#

A state is a named set of property values. Switch states and all those properties change together:

Rectangle {
    id: panel
    property bool open: false
    width: 300; height: 400
    x: -width                                   // default state: hidden off the left edge
    opacity: 0

    states: [
        State {
            name: "open"
            when: panel.open                    // automatic: active while this is true
            PropertyChanges { panel.x: 0; panel.opacity: 1 }    // Qt 6 syntax
        }
    ]
}
  • The default state has the empty name "" and uses the property values written normally.
  • when: activates a state automatically; or set panel.state = "open" manually.
  • PropertyChanges lists what changes. In Qt 6 write target.property: value directly; older code writes PropertyChanges { target: panel; x: 0 }.

Other state elements: AnchorChanges { target: x; anchors.left: … }, ParentChange (re-parent an item), StateChangeScript (run code).

Transitions#

Without transitions, a state change jumps instantly. A transition animates it:

transitions: [
    Transition {
        from: ""; to: "open"                     // opening
        ParallelAnimation {
            NumberAnimation { property: "x"; duration: 350; easing.type: Easing.OutCubic }
            NumberAnimation { property: "opacity"; duration: 250 }
        }
    },
    Transition {
        from: "open"; to: ""                     // closing: faster, accelerating
        NumberAnimation { properties: "x,opacity"; duration: 200; easing.type: Easing.InCubic }
    }
]

Inside a Transition you don't specify to: values. The animation uses the values from the state change. Write from: "*"; to: "*" (the default) to match any change.

Behaviors vs states and transitions#

Use Behavior when… Use States + Transitions when…
one or two properties animate many properties change together
the same animation always applies opening and closing need different animations
changes come from many places you think in named modes (closed/open/expanded)

Most shell code gets far with Behaviors. States shine for multi-mode components like a notification card (collapsed / expanded / dismissing) or a media widget (compact / full).

Animating windows opening and closing#

A Quickshell window that's visible: false isn't drawn, so you can't animate it out after hiding it. The pattern is to keep the window visible while the animation runs:

PanelWindow {
    id: win
    property bool open: GlobalStates.sidebarOpen
    visible: open || slide.running           // stay visible until the slide-out finishes
    color: "transparent"
    implicitWidth: 380
    anchors { top: true; bottom: true; right: true }

    Rectangle {
        id: panel
        width: parent.width; height: parent.height
        x: win.open ? 0 : width               // slide in from the right
        Behavior on x { NumberAnimation { id: slide; duration: 350; easing.type: Easing.OutCubic } }
        color: "#1e1e2e"
    }
}

Here slide.running refers to the animation inside the Behavior; while it runs, the window stays mapped.

View transitions#

Positioners and views have transition slots that animate items as they're added, removed or moved:

Row {
    add: Transition { NumberAnimation { properties: "opacity,scale"; from: 0; to: 1; duration: 200 } }
    move: Transition { NumberAnimation { properties: "x"; duration: 200; easing.type: Easing.OutCubic } }
}

ListView {
    add:       Transition { NumberAnimation { property: "x"; from: 400; duration: 300; easing.type: Easing.OutCubic } }
    remove:    Transition { NumberAnimation { property: "opacity"; to: 0; duration: 200 } }
    displaced: Transition { NumberAnimation { property: "y"; duration: 250; easing.type: Easing.OutCubic } }
    populate:  Transition { NumberAnimation { property: "opacity"; from: 0; to: 1; duration: 300 } }
}

ViewTransition attached properties (ViewTransition.index, ViewTransition.targetIndexes) let you stagger animations, e.g. a delay of ViewTransition.index * 30.

Animators: animations off the main thread#

OpacityAnimator, ScaleAnimator, XAnimator, YAnimator, RotationAnimator and UniformAnimator run on the render thread. They stay smooth even if JavaScript is busy, but they only update the property's value at the end. Use them for continuous effects like spinners:

RotationAnimator on rotation { from: 0; to: 360; duration: 1000; loops: Animation.Infinite; running: busy }

Choreography: a complete expanding card#

ExpandCard.qmlimport QtQuick

Rectangle {
    id: card
    property bool expanded: false
    width: 320
    height: expanded ? 220 : 64
    radius: expanded ? 22 : 32
    color: "#1e1e2e"
    clip: true

    Behavior on height { NumberAnimation { duration: 380; easing.type: Easing.BezierSpline; easing.bezierCurve: [0.05, 0.7, 0.1, 1, 1, 1] } }
    Behavior on radius { NumberAnimation { duration: 380 } }

    Text { x: 20; y: 20; text: "Now playing"; color: "#cdd6f4"; font.bold: true }

    Column {
        x: 20; y: 64; spacing: 8
        opacity: card.expanded ? 1 : 0
        // content fades in AFTER the card has mostly grown, and out quickly
        Behavior on opacity { NumberAnimation { duration: card.expanded ? 250 : 100 } }
        Text { text: "Track title"; color: "white" }
        Text { text: "Artist"; color: "#a6adc8" }
    }

    TapHandler { onTapped: card.expanded = !card.expanded }
}
Exercises
  1. Turn the expanding card into states ("collapsed", "expanded") with different open and close transitions.
  2. Make a Row of chips where new chips scale in (add) and the others slide over (move).
